assumptions_latex: \(p\ge 2\) blocks are given.
All matrices have compatible finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is row-linked block-angular precisely when its only interblock constraint rows are the rows of \((L_1,\ldots,L_p)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional constraint-matrix definition, up to simultaneous row and column permutations.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Structure and Sparsity p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Trust Region Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constraint system in variables \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\) has row-linked block-angular structure if, after row and column permutations, it can be written as \[\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0&\cdots&0\\0&A_2&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&A_p\\L_1&L_2&\cdots&L_p\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\\vdots\\x_p\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\\vdots\\b_p\\d\end{pmatrix}.\] The rows involving \(A_i\) are block-local, while the final row block is the sole constraint interface coupling distinct variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A row-linked system has independent diagonal constraint blocks plus one shared block of linking constraints involving variables from multiple blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Row-Linked Block-Angular Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Structure and Sparsity p. 56
source_witnesses.source_title: Trust Region Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, but the cited locator is only a generic structure-and-sparsity section in the inspectable local table of contents and does not establish the row-linked terminology or displayed normal form. In addition, the conclusion refers to a matrix A that the statement and notation do not introduce. A more specific authoritative source and a notation correction are required.

assumptions_latex: \(p\ge 2\) blocks are given.
All matrices have compatible finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is column-linked block-angular precisely when deleting the shared columns \(y\) leaves a block-diagonal matrix in the local columns.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional constraint-matrix definition, up to simultaneous row and column permutations.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Structure and Sparsity p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Trust Region Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constraint system in variables \((x_1,\ldots,x_p,y)\) has column-linked block-angular structure if, after row and column permutations, it has matrix form \[\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0&\cdots&0&B_1\\0&A_2&\cdots&0&B_2\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&A_p&B_p\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\\vdots\\x_p\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\\vdots\\b_p\end{pmatrix}.\] Each \(x_i\) occurs only in local row block \(i\), whereas the shared variables \(y\) may occur in every row block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A column-linked system becomes block diagonal after removing shared variable columns; those shared variables connect otherwise local row blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Column-Linked Block-Angular Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Structure and Sparsity p. 56
source_witnesses.source_title: Trust Region Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, but the cited generic sparsity locator does not inspectably support the column-linked terminology or exact matrix form. The conclusion also refers to A without introducing it. A specific block-angular source is required before the mathematical formulation can be reviewed conclusively.

children.title: Doubly Linked Block Structure
children.top_down_role: Block geometries containing simultaneous row-linking plus column-linking.

assumptions_latex: \(p\ge 2\) local blocks are given.
All displayed matrices have compatible finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is doubly linked because it contains both shared columns \(y\) and shared linking rows \(\sum_i L_i x_i+My=d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous row- and column-linking form for a finite-dimensional linear constraint system.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Parallelization and Decomposition of Optimization Problems p. 224
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constraint system has doubly linked block structure if, after permutations, it can be represented as \[\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0&\cdots&0&B_1\\0&A_2&\cdots&0&B_2\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&A_p&B_p\\L_1&L_2&\cdots&L_p&M\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\\vdots\\x_p\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\\vdots\\b_p\\d\end{pmatrix}.\] Thus local blocks are coupled through both common variables \(y\) and a linking row block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A doubly linked system simultaneously has shared variable columns and linking constraint rows around otherwise block-diagonal local structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Doubly Linked Block Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Parallelization and Decomposition of Optimization Problems p. 224
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed simultaneous row-and-column linking form is mathematically coherent and definition is the appropriate content kind, but the cited general decomposition section does not inspectably establish the term "doubly linked block structure" or this exact canonical form. A specific source is required.

children.title: Hybrid Block Structure
children.top_down_role: Mixed structural patterns that combine distinct decomposition geometries.

assumptions_latex: Variables and constraints admit finite block partitions.
At least two distinct coupling mechanisms are present.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The structure is hybrid when the quotient incidence graph contains coupling edges of at least two declared types.

notation.meaning: quotient graph induced by block partitions
type assigned to a quotient edge

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-graph definition covering mixtures of row, column, cross, or hierarchical coupling.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Structure and Sparsity p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Trust Region Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(A)\) be the bipartite incidence graph of a constraint matrix \(A\), and contract every prescribed local row block and local column block to obtain a quotient graph \(Q\). Assign each interblock edge \(e\) a type \(\tau(e)\) identifying its coupling mechanism, such as a linking row, shared column, nonlocal cross-link, or parent-child interface. The block structure is hybrid if \[\left|\{\tau(e):e\in E(Q)\}\right|\ge 2.\] This definition concerns structural incidence and does not require coefficients on different coupling types to have equal scale or algebraic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hybrid block structure combines at least two coupling mechanisms, such as linking rows, shared columns, nonlocal cross-links, or hierarchical interfaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Block Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Structure and Sparsity p. 56
source_witnesses.source_title: Trust Region Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition depends on externally "declared" edge types without defining how incidence edges acquire row-linking, shared-column, cross-link, or hierarchical types. Consequently the criterion can change with an arbitrary labeling rather than the matrix structure alone. The cited sparsity locator does not inspectably support this hybrid taxonomy, so a source-grounded formulation is required.

children.title: Cross-Link Interaction
children.top_down_role: Navigation for interactions between multiple linking directions.

assumptions_latex: A matrix \(A\) has prescribed row blocks \(R_i\) and column blocks \(C_j\).
Matrix support is defined by nonzero entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_\times\) exactly records the nonlocal block pairs that prevent the prescribed partition from being block diagonal.

notation.meaning: submatrix on row block i and column block j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-based representation of interactions between prescribed row and column blocks.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Structure and Sparsity p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Trust Region Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For prescribed row blocks \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) and column blocks \(C_1,\ldots,C_p\), define the cross-link set by \[E_\times=\{(i,j):A_{R_i,C_j}\ne 0\ \text{and}\ (i,j)\ \text{is not a designated local block pair}\}.\] The cross-link interaction is represented by the bipartite graph \(G_\times=(\{R_i\}_{i=1}^m,\{C_j\}_{j=1}^p,E_\times)\). An empty \(E_\times\) means that every nonzero block is local under the designation; each edge in \(E_\times\) identifies a direct nonlocal constraint-variable interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-link interaction is the bipartite graph whose edges mark nonzero row-column block pairs outside the designated local blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Link Interaction

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Structure and Sparsity p. 56
source_witnesses.source_title: Trust Region Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate content kind, but the set of designated local block pairs is not introduced mathematically. Without requiring those pairs to be the diagonal matching of a block partition, an empty cross-link set does not imply that the prescribed matrix partition is block diagonal, contrary to the conclusion. The generic sparsity citation does not resolve this ambiguity.

children.title: Nested Block Structure
children.top_down_role: Containment patterns in which decomposable blocks occur within larger blocks.

assumptions_latex: A rooted tree \(T\) indexes a finite family of variable and constraint blocks.
Each descendant subtree induces a well-defined subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The structure is nested exactly when each subtree communicates with its complement only through its ancestral interfaces.

notation.meaning: interface variables associated with node v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-indexed structural definition based on separator containment along ancestor chains.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Parallel Algorithms for Linear Systems with Special Structure p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree-indexed block system has nested block structure if every node \(v\in T\) has an interface set \(S_v\) such that all interactions between blocks in the subtree \(T_v\) and blocks outside \(T_v\) involve only variables or constraints in \[\bigcup_{u\in\operatorname{anc}(v)}S_u,\] where \(\operatorname{anc}(v)\) includes \(v\). Consequently, after the ancestral interfaces are fixed or removed, distinct child subtrees of \(v\) have no direct interaction. The nesting is structural: interfaces may shrink, grow, or overlap along a root-to-leaf path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested block system is tree-indexed, and each subtree connects outward only through interfaces attached to that subtree and its ancestors.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Block Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Parallel Algorithms for Linear Systems with Special Structure p. 110
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition does not specify whether each interface set contains variables, constraints, or incidence-graph vertices, so the assertion that interactions "involve only" their union is not formally determined. The cited section is identified in the local inventory as covering special linear systems, with visible subsections on triangular and tridiagonal systems, and does not inspectably support this tree-separator definition.

children.title: Multilevel Block Structure
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes spanning multiple coordination levels.

assumptions_latex: A rooted tree \(T\) has depth \(L\ge 1\).
Every variable and constraint block is assigned to exactly one tree node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partition is multilevel when direct couplings occur only within nodes or across declared parent-child interfaces at successive levels.

notation.meaning: interface between a node and its parent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite rooted-tree partition with coupling localized to successive hierarchical levels.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Parallel Algorithms for Linear Systems with Special Structure p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A block system has multilevel structure of depth \(L\) if its blocks are indexed by a rooted tree \(T\), with levels \(\ell(v)\in\{0,\ldots,L\}\), and each nonlocal matrix incidence joins a node \(v\) only to its parent through a declared interface \(I_v\). Equivalently, after ordering blocks by subtrees, every off-diagonal nonzero block belongs to a parent-child interface. Removing all interfaces at level \(k\) separates the remaining incidence graph into subtrees rooted below level \(k\), for each \(k\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multilevel system assigns blocks to a rooted tree and confines direct nonlocal coupling to declared interfaces between successive levels.
knowledge_statements.title: Multilevel Block Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Parallel Algorithms for Linear Systems with Special Structure p. 110
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the appropriate role, but the declared interfaces are not specified as vertex sets, edge sets, row blocks, or column blocks, making "removing" them ambiguous. The claimed equivalence and separation conclusion do not follow from parent-child incidence alone without precise separator conditions. The cited special-linear-systems locator does not inspectably support this multilevel formulation.

children.title: Hierarchical Coupling Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces connecting adjacent levels of a hierarchical decomposition.

assumptions_latex: Blocks are indexed by a rooted tree \(T\).
The model has a specified constraint-variable incidence relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_v\) is the complete separator through which the subtree at \(v\) couples to its parent side.

notation.meaning: variables and constraints assigned to a node set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separator interface between a child subtree and the remainder of a tree-indexed model.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Parallel Algorithms for Linear Systems with Special Structure p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonroot node \(v\in T\), a hierarchical coupling interface is a set \(I_v\subseteq B(T_v)\cup B(T\setminus T_v)\) satisfying: every incidence between an element assigned to \(T_v\) and an element assigned outside \(T_v\) has at least one endpoint in \(I_v\). Equivalently, deleting \(I_v\) from the constraint-variable incidence graph disconnects \(B(T_v)\setminus I_v\) from \(B(T\setminus T_v)\setminus I_v\). The interface is minimal when no proper subset of \(I_v\) has this separator property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hierarchical coupling interface is a separator containing every route by which a child subtree interacts with the rest of the model.
knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Coupling Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Parallel Algorithms for Linear Systems with Special Structure p. 110
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The incidence-graph separator definition is internally coherent and definition is the correct content kind, but the cited section does not inspectably support the terminology or the choice to define an interface as a possibly two-sided vertex separator. A source specific to hierarchical block interfaces is required.

children.title: Complicating Variables
children.top_down_role: Variable selections whose placement controls separability across local blocks.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is described by block-local sets and coupling equations.
The variable vector is partitioned as \((y,x_1,\ldots,x_p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\) is complicating precisely when fixing it makes the residual feasible set a Cartesian product of block-local feasible sets.

notation.meaning: local feasible set after fixing y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational definition for variable decomposition of a deterministic finite-dimensional program.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Parallelization and Decomposition of Optimization Problems p. 224
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a feasible set \(F\subseteq Y\times X_1\times\cdots\times X_p\). The variables \(y\in Y\) are complicating variables for the block partition if, for every fixed \(\bar y\in Y\), the fiber factors as \[\{(x_1,\ldots,x_p):(\bar y,x_1,\ldots,x_p)\in F\}=\prod_{i=1}^p X_i(\bar y)\] for suitable block-local sets \(X_i(\bar y)\), whereas the unfixed model contains interactions between at least two blocks through \(y\). Thus fixing \(y\) removes the designated interblock dependence and exposes independent subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complicating variables are shared decisions whose fixation makes the remaining feasible choices separate into independent block-local sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Complicating Variables

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Parallelization and Decomposition of Optimization Problems p. 224
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

children.title: Stage Decisions
children.top_down_role: Decision groupings organized by temporal or informational stage.

assumptions_latex: Stages are indexed by \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\).
Information available at stage \(t\) is represented by \(\mathcal F_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stage decision is feasible only if it belongs to its stage domain and is measurable with respect to information then available.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multistage stochastic-programming sense, including nonanticipativity through measurability.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Parallelization and Decomposition of Optimization Problems p. 224
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a filtered probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t=1}^T,\mathbb P)\), a stage-\(t\) decision is a random vector \(x_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{n_t}\) that is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and satisfies \[x_t(\omega)\in X_t\bigl(x_1(\omega),\ldots,x_{t-1}(\omega),\omega\bigr)\quad\text{for almost every }\omega.\] Measurability imposes nonanticipativity: scenarios indistinguishable under \(\mathcal F_t\) must receive the same stage-\(t\) decision. In a deterministic staged model, \(\mathcal F_t\) may be taken as trivial and the condition reduces to stage-indexed feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stage decision is chosen from its stage-dependent feasible set using only information available by that stage.
knowledge_statements.title: Stage Decisions

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Parallelization and Decomposition of Optimization Problems p. 224
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: On a general filtered probability space, measurability does not literally imply pointwise equality on vaguely described "indistinguishable scenarios" without an atomic or history-based scenario model. Moreover, taking the filtration to be trivial forces an adapted random decision to be essentially constant; it does not merely reduce the definition to stage-indexed feasibility. The cited parallel-decomposition section does not inspectably support this stochastic-programming specialization, so the mathematical version requires an appropriate source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon multistage stochastic decomposition with sampled forward branching, full-scenario backward cuts, and confidence-interval validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(s^t=0\) and impose \(\theta^t=0\) for \(t=1,\ldots,H-1\), with forward sample sets \(F^t\) and branching sets \(B^t\). Repeatedly: (i) solve the first-stage approximation; (ii) for \(t=2,\ldots,H-1\), solve each stage subproblem for every \(x_j^{t-1}\in B^{t-1}\) and \(\xi_k^t\in F^t\), then select \(|B^t|\) successor decisions; and (iii) for \(t=N,\ldots,2\), solve every scenario subproblem at every \(x_j^{t-1}\in B^{t-1}\). From optimal dual vectors \((\pi_{i,m}^t,\sigma_{i,m}^t)\), form \(E^{t-1}=\sum_{i=1}^{M^t}p_i^t\pi_{i,m}^tT_i^{t-1}\) and \(e^{t-1}=\sum_{i=1}^{M^t}p_i^t(\pi_{i,m}^th_i^t+\sigma_{i,m}^te_i^t)\), remove \(\theta^{t-1}=0\) when present, and add \(E^{t-1}x^{t-1}+\theta^{t-1}\ge e^{t-1}\). At \(t=2\), set \(\bar\theta^1=e^1-E^1\widetilde x^1\); repeat the decomposition passes until \(\widetilde\theta^1\) is within the prescribed relative tolerance of \(\bar\theta^1\). Then simulate \(K\) independent \(H\)-stage paths from \(\widetilde x^1\), solve successive stage subproblems, and construct a confidence interval for its expected objective. Stop with \(\widetilde x^1\) when \(c^1\widetilde x^1+\widetilde\theta^1\) lies in that interval; otherwise enlarge the forward and branching samples and repeat. A sequential-sampling rule is required to guarantee termination with a valid confidence interval on \(z^*\), and branching values must be selected carefully; convex combinations of feasible stage-\(t\) values admitting feasible stage-\(t+1\) completions may be consolidated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The abridged nested decomposition method alternates sampled forward passes with backward scenario solves that generate dual recourse cuts. Once the first-stage recourse approximation agrees with its updated bound to relative tolerance, the current first-stage decision is evaluated on independent multistage sample paths. It is accepted when its approximate objective lies in the resulting confidence interval; otherwise the forward and branching samples are enlarged. Valid statistical termination requires sequential sampling, and effective operation requires careful branch selection.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) and \(N\) define finite stage ranges, and the forward sets \(F^t\), branching sets \(B^t\), scenario sets \(\{\xi_i^t\}_{i=1}^{M^t}\), and probabilities \(p_i^t\) are available for the indicated stages.
Every invoked stage subproblem is solvable and supplies an optimal primal solution and, during the backward pass, optimal dual vectors \((\pi_{i,m}^t,\sigma_{i,m}^t)\).
A prescribed relative tolerance and a valid confidence-interval construction for the expected objective are available.
For a termination guarantee with a valid confidence interval on \(z^*\), the sampling sizes are governed by an appropriate sequential-sampling procedure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure either enlarges \(F^t\) and \(B^t\) and repeats, or terminates with \(\widetilde x^1\) when \(c^1\widetilde x^1+\widetilde\theta^1\) belongs to the validation confidence interval; under sequential sampling, the terminating interval is valid for \(z^*\).

children.title: Variable–Stage Partition Interface
children.top_down_role: Compatibility boundaries between complicating-variable choices and stage structure.

assumptions_latex: Variables are assigned to stages \(1,\ldots,T\).
A block partition \(\mathcal B\) of the variable indices is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi\) records exactly which variable blocks intersect which stages and therefore identifies cross-stage blocks.

notation.meaning: stage assignment of variable index j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence representation relating an arbitrary variable partition to a finite stage partition.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Parallelization and Decomposition of Optimization Problems p. 224
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,\ldots,T\}\) assign each variable index to a stage, and let \(\mathcal B=\{B_1,\ldots,B_p\}\) partition the variable indices. The variable-stage partition interface is represented by \[\Pi_{it}=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B_i\cap s^{-1}(t)\ne\varnothing,\qquad \Pi_{it}=0\quad\text{otherwise}.\] A block \(B_i\) is stage-local exactly when \(\sum_{t=1}^T\Pi_{it}=1\); it is cross-stage when this sum exceeds one. Hence \(\Pi\) translates between block decomposition and temporal placement without requiring the two partitions to coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variable-stage interface is a binary incidence matrix showing which variable blocks contain decisions from each stage.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable–Stage Partition Interface

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Parallelization and Decomposition of Optimization Problems p. 224
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary incidence matrix is mathematically well-defined and representation is the correct content kind, but it appears to be a constructed representation rather than a claim inspectably supported by the cited general decomposition section. A source addressing variable-stage partitions or an explicit standard-field rationale is required.

children.title: Complicating Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraint selections whose removal or coordination exposes block separability.

assumptions_latex: \(p\ge 2\) variable blocks are given.
The feasible set is the intersection of block-local constraints and designated coupling constraints.
At least one designated coupling constraint depends on variables from two or more blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraints \(g(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\le 0\) are complicating for the prescribed partition because removing them leaves the Cartesian product \(X_1\times\cdots\times X_p\) of block-local feasible regions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational definition for constraint decomposition of a finite-dimensional program; dual decomposition additionally requires an objective and coupling representation that yield a separable Lagrangian.

source_refs.locator: 3.4.2 Separable Strictly Convex Programming p. 229
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the feasible set \[F=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_p):x_i\in X_i\ \text{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,p\},\ g(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\le 0\}.\] The inequalities \(g(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\le 0\) are complicating constraints for the prescribed partition when at least one component depends on variables from distinct blocks and removing these inequalities leaves exactly the Cartesian product \(X_1\times\cdots\times X_p\). Thus they are the designated constraints preventing blockwise feasibility from being independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complicating constraints are designated interblock restrictions whose removal leaves independent block-local feasible regions.
knowledge_statements.title: Complicating Constraints

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4.2 Separable Strictly Convex Programming p. 229
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

children.title: Shared-Resource Coupling
children.top_down_role: Coupling induced by capacities, budgets, or resources shared across blocks.

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many blocks \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
Each local decision satisfies \(x_i\in X_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\).
Resource usage is affine, with \(A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n_i}\) and shared capacity \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i\le b\) is the shared-resource coupling constraint.

notation.meaning: feasible set and decision of block i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional block-angular inequality form with componentwise resource capacities.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Parallelization and Decomposition of Optimization Problems p. 224
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A shared-resource coupling for block decisions \(x_i\in X_i\) is a constraint of the form \[\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i\le b,\] where the inequality is componentwise. Each vector \(A_i x_i\) is the resource usage attributable to block \(i\), while \(b\) is available capacity shared by all blocks. The constraint is coupling precisely when it cannot be checked from any single \(x_i\) alone, even though the remaining objective and constraints may be block separable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared-resource coupling limits the aggregate resource consumption of otherwise separate decision blocks by a common capacity vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scenario partition \(\mathcal P\) is compatible with information partition \(\mathcal I_t\) and coupling set \(C_t\) when every information-equivalent pair satisfies \[\omega\sim_{\mathcal I_t}\omega'\ \Longrightarrow\ \bigl(\omega\sim_{\mathcal P}\omega'\ \text{or}\ (\omega,\omega')\in C_t\bigr).\] For pairs inside one scenario block, nonanticipativity can be imposed locally. knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Coupling Placement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-based placement rule for graph-partitioned optimization models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have the vertex partition \(V=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{k=1}^K V_k\), and define \(E_k=\{\{u,v\}\in E:u,v\in V_k\}\) and \(E_\partial=E\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^K E_k\). A model term \(h\) is local to block \(k\) when \(S_V(h)\subseteq V_k\) and \(S_E(h)\subseteq E_k\). A term whose support meets more than one block, including any term supported on an edge in \(E_\partial\), is placed on the boundary interface. The decomposition must retain that cross-block dependence through an explicit linking representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Place a term in a local block only when all of its vertex and edge support is internal to that block; otherwise place its cross-block dependence on the explicit boundary interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Function Master Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real partial minimization of finitely many separable subordinate blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), define \(\phi_i(x)=\inf\{q_i(y_i):y_i\in Y_i(x)\}\), using \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Then partial minimization yields \[\inf_{\substack{x\in X\\ y_i\in Y_i(x),\ i=1,\ldots,m}}\left(c(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m q_i(y_i)\right)=\inf_{x\in X}\left(c(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(x)\right).\] The right-hand side also has the epigraph form \[\inf_{\substack{x\in X,\ \theta\in\mathbb{R}^m\\ \theta_i\geq\phi_i(x),\ i=1,\ldots,m}}\left(c(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing every subordinate block at a fixed coordinating decision produces value functions whose sum gives an equivalent master problem; epigraph variables provide an equivalent constrained master form.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) is a positive integer and \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(Y_i(x)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{q_i}\) is the feasible-response set at \(x\), and empty response sets are allowed.
The functions \(c\) and \(q_i\) take values in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and \(\inf_{y_i\in Y_i(x)}q_i(y_i)>-\infty\) whenever \(Y_i(x)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X,\ y_i\in Y_i(x)}\bigl(c(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m q_i(y_i)\bigr)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(c(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(x)\bigr)\), where \(\phi_i(x)=\inf_{y_i\in Y_i(x)}q_i(y_i)\) and \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed-Linking Dual Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex equality-linking Lagrangian dual under a relative-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(F_i=f_i+\delta_{X_i}\). Relaxing \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i=b\) with \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^p\) gives \[g(\lambda)=-\lambda^{\mathsf T}b+\sum_{i=1}^m\inf_{x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}}\bigl(F_i(x_i)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}A_i x_i\bigr).\] Weak duality gives \(\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^p}g(\lambda)\leq p^*\). If the stated relative-interior qualification holds and \(p^*\) is finite, then \[p^*=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^p}g(\lambda),\] so the relaxed-linking dual is an exact separable coordination representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing the common linking equation separates the constrained block objectives; with a finite primal value and the stated relative-interior qualification, the dual and primal values agree.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) is a positive integer, \(A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n_i}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\).
For each \(i\), \(F_i=f_i+\delta_{X_i}:\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The primal value \(p^*=\inf\{\sum_{i=1}^m F_i(x_i):\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i=b\}\) is finite.
The qualification \(b\in\operatorname{ri}(\sum_{i=1}^m A_i\operatorname{dom}F_i)\) holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^p}\{-\lambda^{\mathsf T}b+\sum_{i=1}^m\inf_{x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}}(F_i(x_i)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}A_i x_i)\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Consensus Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensive-form consensus for scenario-separable optimization with one shared decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let scenarios be indexed by \(s\in S\), with weights \(p_s>0\), local objectives \(f_s\), and local feasible sets \(X_s\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). The shared-variable problem \[\min_{z\in\bigcap_{s\in S}X_s}\ \sum_{s\in S}p_s f_s(z)\] has the equivalent scenario-consensus representation \[\min_{z,\,(x_s)_{s\in S}}\ \sum_{s\in S}p_s f_s(x_s)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_s\in X_s,\quad x_s=z\ \text{for every }s\in S.\] Projection onto \(z\) preserves the feasible set and objective value, while each scenario objective and local constraint set remains attached only to its copy \(x_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicate the shared decision once per scenario and impose equality with a common variable; projection recovers exactly the original shared-variable problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Consensus Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-based consensus on a connected undirected coordination graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with an arbitrarily oriented incidence matrix \(B\), and let each vertex \(i\in V\) hold \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Stacking the variables as \(x=(x_i)_{i\in V}\), edge consensus is represented by \[(B^{\mathsf T}\otimes I_n)x=0,\] equivalently \(x_i=x_j\) for every edge \(\{i,j\}\in E\). If \(G\) is connected, then \[\ker(B^{\mathsf T}\otimes I_n)=\{\mathbf{1}_{|V|}\otimes z:z\in\mathbb{R}^n\},\] so the edge constraints are equivalent to global consensus. For a disconnected graph, they impose consensus only within each connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incidence-matrix constraints enforce equality across edges; on a connected graph they are exactly equivalent to one common decision at every vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
\(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\) for every \(i\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(G\) is connected, then \((B^{\mathsf T}\otimes I_n)x=0\) if and only if \(x=\mathbf{1}_{|V|}\otimes z\) for some \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus-Topology Crosswalk

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) index scenario copies \(x_s\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(G=(S,E)\) have incidence matrix \(B\). knowledge_statements.title: Small Coupling with Large Local Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-angular linear programs whose interface dimension is small relative to local dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a block-angular problem \[\min\ \sum_{i=1}^N c_i^{\mathsf T}x_i\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_i\in X_i,\quad \sum_{i=1}^N A_i x_i=b,\] where each \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) is a large local polyhedron and the coupling equation has \(r\) rows. When \(r\ll\sum_i n_i\), a decomposition representation can keep every \(X_i\) local and communicate only interface quantities in \(\mathbb{R}^r\), such as \(A_i x_i\), multipliers, or cuts. The representation advantage is structural: local formulation size is separated from the dimension of the coordinating space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a few equations couple very large polyhedral blocks, decomposition retains the blocks locally and coordinates through only low-dimensional interface information.
assumptions_latex: \(X_i\) is a nonempty polyhedron for each \(i\).
The only cross-block constraints are \(\sum_i A_i x_i=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupling information lies in an \(r\)-dimensional space even when \(\sum_i n_i\) is large.

notation.meaning: local feasible polyhedron of block i
local contribution to the coupling equations

source_refs.source_title: Practical Methods of Optimization
source_refs.locator: 8.5 Stable and Large-scale Linear Programming p. 168

source_witnesses.source_title: Practical Methods of Optimization
source_witnesses.locator: 8.5 Stable and Large-scale Linear Programming p. 168

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The structural principle is plausible, but the cited general large-scale linear-programming section is not clearly specific to block-angular decomposition or communication through an r-dimensional interface. A direct decomposition locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Huge Implicit Local Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which explicit local-model materialization exceeds available resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For local block \(i\), let an explicit representation require \(m_i\) stored scalars, let \(M_i\) be its storage budget, and suppose an oracle can evaluate the needed local products, constraints, or subproblem solutions without materializing all \(m_i\) entries. Explicit monolithic or decomposition implementations that require the full local representation are infeasible whenever \(m_i>M_i\) for some \(i\). A viable representation must instead expose an oracle interface whose working storage \(w_i\) satisfies \(w_i\le M_i\). Decomposition alone does not remove this boundary if each local solver still constructs the prohibited explicit block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If any explicit local block exceeds its storage budget, decomposition helps only when local computations themselves use an implicit, matrix-free, or oracle representation.
assumptions_latex: Each local block has a finite storage budget \(M_i\).
Required local operations are available through an implicit oracle using working storage \(w_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_i>M_i\) rules out full materialization; feasibility requires an implementation with \(w_i\le M_i\).

notation.meaning: storage required by the explicit local formulation
available storage budget for block i
working storage of the implicit oracle

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary fits the terminal container, but no evidence supports the claimed necessity of the oracle-storage condition or the matrix-free implementation distinction.

knowledge_statements.title: Many Scenarios with Shared Histories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonanticipativity represented by equivalence classes induced by common scenario histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite scenario set over stages \(t=0,\ldots,T\), and let \(x_{s,t}\) be the decision copy for scenario \(s\) at stage \(t\). Define \(s\sim_t s'\) when scenarios \(s\) and \(s'\) have identical information histories through stage \(t\). Nonanticipativity is the constraint system \[x_{s,t}=x_{s',t}\quad\text{whenever}\quad s\sim_t s'.\] Equivalently, introduce one variable \(z_{C,t}\) for each equivalence class \(C\in S/{\sim_t}\) and impose \(x_{s,t}=z_{C,t}\) for \(s\in C\). This class representation avoids unnecessary pairwise equalities while preserving exactly the adapted decision set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenarios sharing the same observed history must share their stage decision; one variable per history class compactly enforces this nonanticipativity.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and the stage set are finite.
\(\sim_t\) is equality of information histories through stage \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pairwise nonanticipativity and one-variable-per-history-class representations define the same decisions.

notation.meaning: decision for scenario s at stage t
equivalence relation of shared histories through stage t
decision associated with history class C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The history-class representation is standard, but the exact stage-information convention for nonanticipativity is source-dependent and no stochastic-programming locator is supplied.

children.title: Monolithic Formulation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases favoring a unified formulation without structural decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Monolithic Formulation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource-and-cost condition for retaining all blocks in one solver model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_{\mathrm{mono}}\) be a monolithic formulation equivalent to a given structured problem, let \(M(F_{\mathrm{mono}})\) denote its predicted peak memory, and let \(T(F_{\mathrm{mono}})\) denote its predicted solution cost. Given memory budget \(M_{\max}\) and competing admissible representations \(\mathcal{R}\), the problem lies in the monolithic-selection regime under this cost model when \[M(F_{\mathrm{mono}})\le M_{\max}\quad\text{and}\quad T(F_{\mathrm{mono}})\le T(R)\ \text{for every }R\in\mathcal{R}.\] Equivalence requires that the monolithic variables and constraints project onto the original feasible set with the same objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monolithic model is selected when it is equivalent, fits memory, and has no greater predicted solution cost than any admitted alternative representation.
assumptions_latex: All compared representations are mathematically equivalent.
The estimates \(M\) and \(T\) use the same computational environment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The monolithic regime is characterized by feasibility of its resource budget and cost dominance within \(\mathcal{R}\).

notation.meaning: predicted peak memory of formulation F
predicted solution cost of formulation F

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is an appropriate content kind, but this is a stipulated selection rule under a predictive cost model rather than an established source-backed regime characterization. A supporting locator is required.

children.title: Hybrid Formulation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases combining monolithic components with decomposed components.

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Formulation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial aggregation within groups combined with decomposition across groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition block indices \(I\) into nonempty groups \(I_1,\ldots,I_K\). For a structured problem with local constraints \(x_i\in X_i\) and coupling \(\sum_{i\in I}A_i x_i=b\), define group variables \(u_k=(x_i)_{i\in I_k}\), group feasible sets \(U_k=\prod_{i\in I_k}X_i\), and group coupling maps \(D_k u_k=\sum_{i\in I_k}A_i x_i\). The equivalent hybrid representation is \[u_k\in U_k\quad(k=1,\ldots,K),\qquad \sum_{k=1}^K D_k u_k=b.\] It is monolithic within each group and decomposed between groups; singleton groups recover block decomposition, while \(K=1\) recovers the monolithic formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hybrid formulations aggregate selected blocks into groups, solve each group monolithically, and retain decomposition only across group interfaces.
assumptions_latex: \(I_1,\ldots,I_K\) form a partition of \(I\).
All cross-block dependence is represented by \(\sum_i A_i x_i=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Grouping preserves the original feasible set under the identification \(u_k=(x_i)_{i\in I_k}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The grouped formulation is algebraically coherent and representation is the correct kind, but no authoritative source supports its designation and interpretation as a hybrid formulation regime.

children.title: Regime-Transition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural thresholds affecting movement between unified and hybrid formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Regime-Transition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost or resource equalities separating monolithic and hybrid representation choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda\) parameterize problem size, coupling density, or available resources. For equivalent monolithic and hybrid representations, let \(T_M(\lambda)\), \(T_H(\lambda)\) be predicted solution costs and \(M_M(\lambda)\), \(M_H(\lambda)\) predicted peak memories under a common environment with budget \(M_{\max}(\lambda)\). A cost-driven transition occurs at any \(\lambda^*\) satisfying \[T_M(\lambda^*)=T_H(\lambda^*)\] when both representations fit memory and the sign of \(T_M-T_H\) changes locally. A resource-driven transition occurs when one memory function crosses \(M_{\max}\), thereby entering or leaving the admissible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime boundary occurs where equivalent formulations exchange predicted cost dominance or where one formulation crosses the available resource limit.
assumptions_latex: The compared formulations are mathematically equivalent.
Cost and memory predictions use a common computational model.
The parameter \(\lambda\) varies over a specified domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transition points satisfy a dominance tie with sign change or an admissibility equality \(M_R(\lambda^*)=M_{\max}(\lambda^*)\).

notation.meaning: predicted peak memory of representation R

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and a resource crossing need not occur at an equality without continuity or an equivalent regularity assumption. The exact transition criterion therefore remains unreliable.

children.title: LP Polyhedral Decomposition Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Continuous linear decomposition organized by the representation of the linking structure and the polyhedral certificates exchanged with the coordinator.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Linear Benders Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cutting-plane Benders method for a two-block linear program with continuous recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x+q^{\mathsf T}y:x\in X,\ Wy\ge h-Tx,\ y\ge0\}\), where \(X\) is a polyhedron. Initialize a master with \(x\in X\), a recourse variable \(\theta\), and any valid lower bound on \(\theta\). At iteration \(k\), solve the master and then the recourse LP at \(x^k\). If recourse is infeasible, obtain an extreme ray \(r^k\ge0\), \(W^{\mathsf T}r^k\le0\), and add \((r^k)^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\le0\). Otherwise obtain an optimal dual vector \(\pi^k\ge0\), \(W^{\mathsf T}\pi^k\le q\), and add \(\theta\ge(\pi^k)^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\). Stop when the incumbent upper bound minus the master lower bound is at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve a master and recourse LP, adding feasibility rays or optimality cuts until the certified lower–upper bound gap meets tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
Every feasible bounded recourse LP satisfies strong linear-programming duality.
A finite valid initial lower bound for recourse is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an incumbent \((x,y)\) whose certified objective gap is at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: master lower approximation of recourse value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut formulas have the correct signs, but no Benders locator supports the algorithm. The stated output guarantee also requires conditions addressing finite optimal value, availability of incumbents, exact solves, and finite termination or must be made conditional on termination.

knowledge_statements.title: Benders Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas-ray certificate for infeasible linear recourse at a master point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a master point \(\bar x\) and consider the recourse system \(Wy\ge h-T\bar x\), \(y\ge0\). A Benders feasibility certificate is a vector \(r\) satisfying \[r\ge0,\qquad W^{\mathsf T}r\le0,
\qquad r^{\mathsf T}(h-T\bar x)>0.\] These inequalities are directly checkable and certify that the recourse system has no feasible \(y\). Moreover, the associated Benders feasibility cut \[r^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\le0\] is valid for every master point whose recourse system is feasible and excludes \(\bar x\). Extreme rays of \(\{r:r\ge0,\ W^{\mathsf T}r\le0\}\) provide the standard irreducible cut family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative dual ray with positive residual proves recourse infeasibility and yields a valid master cut excluding the failed point.
assumptions_latex: The recourse constraints are \(Wy\ge h-Tx\) with \(y\ge0\).
All data are finite-dimensional real matrices and vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed \(r\) certifies infeasibility at \(\bar x\), and \(r^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\le0\) is valid for feasible recourse.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed Farkas certificate and feasibility cut are correct for the stated recourse system, but no source is provided. The description of extreme-ray cuts as an irreducible family also requires definition and support.

knowledge_statements.title: Benders Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual recourse solution certifying a globally valid Benders optimality cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a master point \(\bar x\) with finite recourse value \[Q(\bar x)=\min\{q^{\mathsf T}y:Wy\ge h-T\bar x,\ y\ge0\},\] let \(\bar\pi\) satisfy \(\bar\pi\ge0\), \(W^{\mathsf T}\bar\pi\le q\), and \(\bar\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-T\bar x)=Q(\bar x)\). Dual feasibility makes \[Q(x)\ge\bar\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\] valid for every \(x\). Hence \(\theta\ge\bar\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\) is a Benders optimality cut, tight at \(\bar x\). A primal recourse solution \(\bar y\) together with \(\bar\pi\) and equality of their objective values is a finite, directly checkable optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal recourse dual vector defines a globally valid lower cut; matching primal and dual values certify recourse optimality and cut tightness.
assumptions_latex: The recourse LP at \(\bar x\) is feasible and has finite value.
Strong duality holds for the recourse primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta\ge\bar\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\) is globally valid and is tight at \(x=\bar x\).

notation.meaning: optimal recourse value at master point x
optimal dual recourse vector at the candidate point
master approximation of the recourse value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual-feasibility inequality, cut validity, and primal-dual certificate are mathematically consistent, and certificate is the correct content kind, but a direct Benders optimality-certificate locator is required.

children.title: Single-Cut Benders
children.top_down_role: Benders variants using a single aggregated cut contribution per master iteration.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Cut Benders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregated optimality cuts for finite separable recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the recourse function be \(Q(x)=\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(x)\), where \(p_s>0\) and \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\). If \(\ell_s^k(x)=a_s^k+(b_s^k)^{\mathsf T}x\le Q_s(x)\) is a valid scenario cut, single-cut Benders uses one epigraph variable \(\theta\) and the aggregate inequality \[\theta\ge \sum_{s\in S}p_s\ell_s^k(x).\] The master problem minimizes \(c^{\mathsf T}x+\theta\) over \(x\in X\) and all accumulated aggregate cuts. Thus one master inequality represents the weighted recourse information produced at iteration \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Single-cut Benders combines all scenario underestimators generated in an iteration into one weighted inequality for a single recourse variable.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite, \(X\neq\varnothing\), and \(p_s>0\) with \(\sum_s p_s=1\).
Each \(\ell_s^k\) is a globally valid affine underestimator of \(Q_s\) on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta\ge\sum_{s\in S}p_s\ell_s^k(x)\) is valid for \(\theta\ge Q(x)\).

notation.meaning: recourse value of scenario or block s

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically plausible and fits the Single-Cut Benders leaf, but no inspectable Benders source or locator supports the aggregation convention, master formulation, or validity claim.

children.title: Multicut Benders
children.top_down_role: Benders variants retaining separate cut contributions from multiple subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Multicut Benders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disaggregated optimality cuts for finite separable recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q(x)=\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(x)\), introduce an epigraph variable \(\theta_s\) for every scenario or independent recourse block. Given valid affine underestimators \(\ell_s^k(x)\le Q_s(x)\), the multicut master imposes \[\theta_s\ge \ell_s^k(x)\qquad(s\in S)\] and minimizes \(c^{\mathsf T}x+\sum_{s\in S}p_s\theta_s\) over \(x\in X\) and all accumulated cuts. Each block therefore contributes a separate master inequality at an iteration, rather than being combined before insertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multicut Benders retains a separate epigraph variable and cut for every scenario or independent recourse block.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite and the recourse objective is additively separable across \(S\).
Each \(\ell_s^k\) is a valid affine underestimator of \(Q_s\) on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(\theta_s\ge\ell_s^k(x)\) jointly imply \(\sum_s p_s\theta_s\ge\sum_s p_s\ell_s^k(x)\).

notation.meaning: block cut generated at iteration k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The disaggregated representation fits the Multicut Benders leaf and is internally coherent, but it has no authoritative source with a specific locator supporting the blockwise epigraph formulation.

children.title: Cut-Granularity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Navigation across master size, certificate granularity, and subproblem separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Granularity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Master-strength comparison for matched valid scenario cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix scenario cuts \(\ell_s^k\) and weights \(p_s>0\). The multicut system \(\theta_s\ge\ell_s^k(x)\) implies the matched single-cut inequality \(\theta\ge\sum_s p_s\ell_s^k(x)\) under \(\theta=\sum_s p_s\theta_s\). Consequently, after projection onto \((x,\theta)\), the multicut relaxation is contained in the single-cut relaxation, and its minimization lower bound is no smaller. This ordering concerns relaxation strength for the same cuts; it does not order total runtime, because finer cuts enlarge the master and increase storage and reoptimization cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finer disaggregation strengthens the matched master relaxation but adds variables and constraints, so relaxation strength alone does not determine runtime.
assumptions_latex: Both masters use the same set of valid block cuts and the same feasible set \(X\).
The problem is minimized and \(p_s>0\) for every \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{multi}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{single}}\) after projection, hence \(L_{\mathrm{multi}}\ge L_{\mathrm{single}}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matched-cut relaxation ordering is plausible and the property kind fits this tradeoff leaf. The additional runtime, storage, and reoptimization claims require a Benders-specific source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Partial Cut Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Intermediate cut groupings between full aggregation and fully disaggregated cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Cut Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Groupwise aggregation between single-cut and multicut formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G\) be a partition of the finite block set \(S\). Associate one variable \(\theta_g\) with each \(g\in\mathcal G\). From valid block cuts \(\ell_s^k(x)\le Q_s(x)\), impose \[\theta_g\ge\sum_{s\in g}p_s\ell_s^k(x)\qquad(g\in\mathcal G),\] and use \(\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}\theta_g\) as the recourse term in the master objective. The partition \(\{S\}\) gives single-cut aggregation, whereas the singleton partition gives the multicut formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial aggregation creates one recourse variable and one aggregated cut per chosen group of subproblems.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is a partition of \(S\).
Each \(\ell_s^k\) is valid for \(Q_s\), and the weights \(p_s\) are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every group cut underestimates \(\sum_{s\in g}p_sQ_s(x)\), and the group objectives sum to an underestimator of \(Q(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partition-based representation appropriately interpolates between single-cut and multicut formulations, but no cited source establishes this partial-aggregation formulation or its endpoint conventions.

children.title: Multiple Benders Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Decompositions containing several independently coordinated Benders subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Benders Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive recourse decomposed into independently solvable value functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the second-stage variables and constraints split into independent blocks \(s\in S\): \[Q(x)=\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(x),\qquad Q_s(x)=\inf_{y_s}\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y_s:W_sy_s\ge h_s-T_sx\}.\] For a fixed master point \(x^k\), every finite block problem may be solved independently. A dual feasible vector \(\pi_s^k\ge0\) satisfying \(W_s^{\mathsf T}\pi_s^k=q_s\) yields the valid affine cut \(Q_s(x)\ge(\pi_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\). These block cuts may be retained separately or aggregated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Additively separable recourse permits independent Benders subproblems whose dual solutions generate block-specific affine cuts.
assumptions_latex: The recourse feasible set and objective separate by \(s\) once \(x\) is fixed.
Each displayed block linear program has finite value where an optimality cut is generated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each dual-feasible \(\pi_s^k\) defines a globally valid lower affine bound for \(Q_s\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf, but the domain and sign restrictions of the primal variables are not stated, so the displayed dual feasibility conditions cannot be checked unambiguously. A specific Benders-duality source is also absent.

children.title: Aggregation–Subproblem Alignment
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between cut groups and the underlying subproblem partition.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation–Subproblem Alignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition between recourse blocks and aggregation groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) index independently solved subproblems and let \(\mathcal G\) index master epigraph variables. Aggregation is aligned when there is a partition \(\{S_g:g\in\mathcal G\}\) of \(S\) such that \[Q_g(x)=\sum_{s\in S_g}p_sQ_s(x),\qquad \theta_g\ge
a_g^k+(b_g^k)^{\mathsf T}x,\] with \(a_g^k=\sum_{s\in S_g}p_sa_s^k\) and \(b_g^k=\sum_{s\in S_g}p_sb_s^k\) whenever \(a_s^k+(b_s^k)^{\mathsf T}x\le Q_s(x)\). Thus every subproblem contributes exactly once to exactly one group cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alignment requires each independently solved block to belong to exactly one aggregation group, with group cuts equal to weighted sums of constituent cuts.
assumptions_latex: The recourse function is \(Q(x)=\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(x)\).
All constituent affine cuts are valid on the same master domain \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{S_g:g\in\mathcal G\}\) must partition \(S\), and group-cut coefficients must equal the weighted sums of constituent coefficients.

notation.meaning: subproblem indices assigned to group g

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed partition and coefficient-summing condition is coherent and the condition kind fits the leaf. It is nevertheless presented as a required alignment convention without an authoritative source or locator.

children.title: Pareto-Optimal Cut Families
children.top_down_role: Cut families organized by dominance quality within the relevant master representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Pareto-Optimal Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto optimality under pointwise cut dominance on the master domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\mathcal C\) be a family of valid affine underestimators of a value function \(Q\) on \(X\). For \(\ell_1,
\ell_2\in\mathcal C\), say that \(\ell_1\) dominates \(\ell_2\) when \(\ell_1(x)\ge\ell_2(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), with strict inequality for at least one \(x\in X\). A cut \(\theta\ge\ell(x)\) is Pareto-optimal in \(\mathcal C\) if no other member of \(\mathcal C\) dominates \(\ell\). A Pareto-optimal cut family consists entirely of such undominated cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Benders cut is Pareto-optimal when no other valid cut in the comparison family is everywhere at least as strong and somewhere stronger.
assumptions_latex: Every \(\ell\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(\ell(x)\le Q(x)\) for all \(x\in X\).
Dominance is evaluated on the specified master domain \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell\) is Pareto-optimal exactly when no \(\widehat\ell\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(\widehat\ell\ge\ell\) on \(X\) with strict inequality somewhere.

notation.meaning: comparison family of valid affine cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally precise relative to the declared comparison family and domain, and its content kind fits the leaf. An authoritative locator is required to confirm that it matches the intended Benders-specific notion of Pareto optimality.

children.title: Lifted Cut Families
children.top_down_role: Cut families strengthened through higher-dimensional or enriched representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benders-valid inequalities expressed in an extended master formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\subseteq X\times Z\) be an extended master set whose projection onto \(X\) is \(X\). A lifted Benders cut is an inequality \[\theta\ge a+b^{\mathsf T}x+d^{\mathsf T}z\] valid for every \((x,z)\in E\) and every feasible epigraph point satisfying \(\theta\ge Q(x)\). Its projection induces the valid inequality \(\theta\ge\inf\{a+b^{\mathsf T}x+d^{\mathsf T}z:(x,z)\in E\}\) on \(X\). A lifted cut family is a collection of such inequalities using auxiliary variables or valid linking relations to strengthen the extended master.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted cut uses auxiliary master variables and linking constraints while remaining valid for every feasible epigraph point of the recourse function.
assumptions_latex: \(E\subseteq X\times Z\) is nonempty on every fiber and projects onto \(X\).
The lifted inequality is valid for the extended representation of the original feasible epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projecting the lifted inequality and \(E\) onto \((x,\theta)\) preserves validity for \(\theta\ge Q(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition describes a generic extended-formulation cut, but 'lifted Benders cut' has specialized meanings. Without a source, it is uncertain that this construction matches the exact local family intended by the taxonomy.

children.title: Cut-Dominance Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Comparative scope for dominance, lifting strength, and representation dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Dominance Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of global dominance comparisons between affine cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For affine cuts \(\theta\ge\ell_i(x)=a_i+b_i^{\mathsf T}x\), dominance is relative to the chosen master domain \(X\). If there exist \(x^+,x^-\in X\) such that \(\ell_1(x^+)>
\ell_2(x^+)\) and \(\ell_1(x^-)<\ell_2(x^-)\), neither cut dominates the other on \(X\), although either may be stronger near a particular incumbent. Moreover, dominance on a restricted region \(R\subset X\) need not extend to \(X\). Hence local cut strength, violation at one point, or a larger intercept alone does not certify global dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two cuts are incomparable when their affine values cross on the master domain; dominance on a local region need not hold globally.
assumptions_latex: Both affine inequalities are valid cuts for the same epigraph and are compared on the same set \(X\).
The points \(x^+\) and \(x^-\) belong to \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Opposite strict inequalities at \(x^+\) and \(x^-\) preclude either \(\ell_1\) or \(\ell_2\) from dominating the other on \(X\).

notation.meaning: affine right-hand side of cut i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The crossing argument correctly identifies a boundary of global affine-cut dominance, and failure_boundary is the appropriate kind. No inspectable source supports its placement as a Benders cut-dominance boundary.

children.title: Regularized Benders Variants
children.top_down_role: Benders variants using regularization to control master-point movement.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Benders Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal stabilization of trial-point selection in the Benders master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x^0\in X\), \(\rho_k>0\), and a cutting model \(m_k(x)\le Q(x)\), compute \[x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{c^{\mathsf T}x+m_k(x)+\frac{\rho_k}{2}\|x-x^k_c\|^2\right\}.\] Evaluate the Benders subproblem at \(x^{k+1}\), append valid optimality or feasibility cuts to form \(m_{k+1}\), and update the center \(x_c^k\) according to the chosen serious-step rule. Compute the lower bound from the unregularized cutting master. Stop when a certified feasible upper bound minus this lower bound is at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularized Benders selects trial points by adding a proximal penalty around a center while retaining unregularized bounds for certification.
assumptions_latex: Every appended cut is globally valid on \(X\).
The regularized trial problem attains a minimizer and \(\rho_k>0\).
Upper and lower bounds refer to the original unregularized objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an incumbent whose certified gap satisfies \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct kind for this variant leaf, but the serious-step and center-update rules are left unspecified, and no source identifies the precise regularized Benders variant or validates its certification procedure.

children.title: Level-Based Benders Variants
children.top_down_role: Benders variants organized around level-based stabilization regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Based Benders Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-set stabilization using projected trial points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Maintain a cutting model \(f_k(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x+m_k(x)\), a lower bound \(L_k=
\min_{x\in X}f_k(x)\), an incumbent upper bound \(U_k\), and a center \(x_c^k\). Choose \(\lambda_k\in(0,1)\) and set \(v_k=L_k+
\lambda_k(U_k-L_k)\). Compute \[x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\{\|x-x_c^k\|^2:f_k(x)\le v_k\}.\] Evaluate the subproblems, add valid cuts, update the bounds and center, and stop when \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\). If the level set is empty, raise the lower bound and select a new level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Level Benders projects a center onto an intermediate cutting-model level set, then updates cuts and certified bounds.
assumptions_latex: The cutting model globally underestimates the original objective on \(X\).
A finite incumbent bound \(U_k\) is available when the level is formed.
The projection subproblem is solved exactly or to a certified tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination returns an incumbent with certified objective gap at most \(\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The level-projection scheme is plausible and algorithm is the correct kind, but the empty-level lower-bound update and center rules are unspecified. A variant-specific convergence or algorithm source is required.

children.title: Inexact Benders Variants
children.top_down_role: Benders variants permitting controlled inexactness in coordination or subproblem processing.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Benders Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benders iteration with certified approximate subproblem information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At master point \(x^k\), let an inexact oracle return an affine function \(\ell_k\), an estimate \(\widehat Q_k\), and certified errors \(\delta_k,\eta_k\ge0\) satisfying \[\ell_k(x)\le Q(x)\quad(x\in X),\qquad Q(x^k)\le\widehat Q_k+
\eta_k,\qquad \widehat Q_k-
\ell_k(x^k)\le\delta_k.\] Append the valid cut \(\theta\ge\ell_k(x)\), update the feasible upper bound using \(\widehat Q_k+
\eta_k\), and solve the master for the next point. Stop only when the certified upper bound minus the master lower bound is at most \(\varepsilon\); otherwise require the oracle errors to be reduced according to the prescribed accuracy schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact Benders accepts approximate subproblem solutions only with error certificates that preserve valid cuts and a reliable global optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: The oracle cut \(\ell_k\) is globally valid despite inexact subproblem solution.
The reported \(\delta_k\) and \(\eta_k\) are computable upper bounds on the stated errors.
The master problem is solved to a certified lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the stopping test holds, the returned feasible incumbent has objective error at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: oracle cut-gap certificate at the query point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certified-oracle formulation fits an algorithm leaf, but inexact Benders error models vary across references and the required accuracy schedule is not defined. The mathematical version and termination guarantees therefore require a specific source.

children.title: Stabilization-Accuracy Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits governing compatibility between stabilization choices and inexact information.

knowledge_statements.title: Stabilization-Accuracy Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between stabilized trial-point selection and valid Benders bounds or termination certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be the recourse function and let \(m_k\le Q\) be the current Benders cutting-plane model on the master domain \(X\). A stabilization term may select the next trial point, but a certified lower bound must remain \(L_k=\inf_{x\in X}\{c^{\mathsf T}x+m_k(x)\}\), excluding any artificial stabilization penalty. If cuts or subproblem values have certified aggregate error at most \(\varepsilon_k\), termination with incumbent value \(U_k\) is valid only when \(U_k-L_k\le \tau-\varepsilon_k\). Using the stabilized objective itself as \(L_k\), or ignoring \(\varepsilon_k\), can falsely certify \(\tau\)-optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stabilization may choose trial points, but valid bounds must use the unstabilized model and termination must explicitly absorb certified inexactness.
assumptions_latex: \(m_k(x)\le Q(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
\(U_k\) is the value of a feasible incumbent.
\(\varepsilon_k\ge 0\) bounds all error entering the reported gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_k-L_k\le \tau-\varepsilon_k\) is sufficient for a certified gap of at most \(\tau\); the stated substitutions need not be valid.

notation.meaning: Certified lower bound and feasible incumbent value

review_flags: Exact stabilization and inexact-cut conventions vary; a decomposition-specific source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but no decomposition-specific source supports the aggregate-error convention or the termination formula. The meaning of ε_k must be tied to a cited inexact-cut or oracle model.
