children.title: History Equivalence Classes
children.top_down_role: Groupings of scenarios sharing indistinguishable information histories.

assumptions_latex: A finite scenario set \(\Omega\) is equipped with stagewise history maps \(H_t:\Omega\to\mathcal H_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relation \(\sim_t\) partitions \(\Omega\) into the scenarios indistinguishable at stage \(t\).

notation.meaning: Equality of observed histories through stage t

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports scenario-history equivalence classes.
A finite scenario-tree reference is required for source certification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario equivalence induced by equality of observed histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each stage \(t\), define a relation on \(\Omega\) by \[\omega\sim_t\omega'\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H_t(\omega)=H_t(\omega').\] This is an equivalence relation. Its class \([\omega]_t=\{\omega'\in\Omega:H_t(\omega')=H_t(\omega)\}\) contains precisely the scenarios indistinguishable from \(\omega\) using stage-\(t\) information. If histories accumulate information, then \(\omega\sim_{t+1}\omega'\) implies \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\), so the induced partitions refine with time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenarios are history-equivalent at a stage when they have identical observed histories; these equivalence classes form a partition that refines over time.
knowledge_statements.title: History Equivalence Classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivalence-class definition is correct in form, but no source is cited. A source should also state the accumulated-history condition underlying refinement over time.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stage-\(t\) scenario-tree node \(n\in\mathcal N_t\) is an information state corresponding to one realized history through stage \(t\). assumptions_latex: A finite scenario tree has scenario set \(\Omega\) and node map \(n_t:\Omega\to\mathcal N_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bundles \(B_{t,n}\) form the stage-\(t\) information partition of \(\Omega\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bundles induced by common scenario-tree nodes, not arbitrary scenario clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a stage \(t\) and node \(n\in\mathcal N_t\), the associated scenario bundle is \[B_{t,n}=\{\omega\in\Omega:n_t(\omega)=n\}.\] The nonempty family \(\{B_{t,n}:n\in\mathcal N_t\}\) partitions \(\Omega\). If the tree records accumulated information, then every bundle at stage \(t+1\) is contained in exactly one bundle at stage \(t\). Scenario-indexed decisions are nonanticipative precisely when they are constant on every bundle \(B_{t,n}\) at the corresponding stage.

children.title: History–Bundle Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Boundaries determining whether scenario bundles preserve information distinctions.

assumptions_latex: Stagewise histories \(H_t\) and a finite-tree node map \(n_t\) are defined on the same scenario set \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility holds exactly when node fibers and history fibers coincide at every stage.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact compatibility between histories, nodes, and node-induced bundles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The history and bundle representations are compatible if, for every stage \(t\) and scenarios \(\omega,\omega'\in\Omega\), \[H_t(\omega)=H_t(\omega')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n_t(\omega)=n_t(\omega').\] Equivalently, every nonempty bundle \(B_{t,n}\) is exactly one equivalence class of the relation induced by \(H_t\), and every such class is a bundle. Under this condition, a decision is constant on stage-\(t\) histories if and only if it is constant on stage-\(t\) bundles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Histories and bundles are compatible when two scenarios share a node exactly when they share the same observed history.

children.title: Consensus-Subspace Language
children.top_down_role: Vocabulary for nonanticipative decisions viewed through agreement subspaces.

Scenario-indexed decisions lie in the product Hilbert space \(\mathcal X=\prod_{\omega\in\Omega}\mathbb R^d\).
A partition \(\mathcal B\) groups scenarios having the same available information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The consensus set \(\mathcal C\) is a closed linear subspace encoding equality within every information bundle.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The consensus subspace associated with \(\mathcal B\) is \[\mathcal C=\{x=(x^\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega}\in\mathcal X:x^\omega=x^{\omega'}\text{ whenever }\omega,\omega'\in B\text{ for some }B\in\mathcal B\}.\] It is a closed linear subspace of \(\mathcal X\). Membership in \(\mathcal C\) is exactly the scenario-indexed nonanticipativity condition for the information partition \(\mathcal B\); each bundle has one common decision value, although different bundles may have different values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The consensus subspace consists of scenario-indexed decisions that agree within every bundle of scenarios sharing the same information.

children.title: Projection Language
children.top_down_role: Vocabulary for mappings from scenario decisions toward admissible agreement structure.

assumptions_latex: The product space \(\mathcal X=\prod_{\omega\in\Omega}\mathbb R^d\) has weighted inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle_p=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p_\omega\langle x^\omega,y^\omega\rangle\), where \(p_\omega>0\).
The partition \(\mathcal B\) defines the consensus subspace \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The orthogonal projection onto \(\mathcal C\) replaces each scenario component by its probability-weighted bundle average.

notation.meaning: Weighted orthogonal projection onto the consensus subspace

review_flags: The projection formula specializes the cited projection theorem to a weighted bundle-consensus subspace.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted orthogonal projection for finite scenario bundles.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Optimality Conditions and the Projection Theorem p. 210
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B\in\mathcal B\), let \(p(B)=\sum_{\omega\in B}p_\omega\). The weighted orthogonal projection of \(x\in\mathcal X\) onto \(\mathcal C\) is given componentwise by \[(P_{\mathcal C}x)^\omega=\frac{1}{p(B(\omega))}\sum_{\omega'\in B(\omega)}p_{\omega'}x^{\omega'}.\] Thus projection replaces all components in a bundle by their conditional probability-weighted average. It is the unique minimizer of \(\min_{z\in\mathcal C}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p_\omega\lVert z^\omega-x^\omega\rVert^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto consensus replaces every scenario decision by the probability-weighted average over its information bundle.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Language

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Optimality Conditions and the Projection Theorem p. 210
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consensus membership is equivalent to being a fixed point of \(P_{\mathcal C}\), while the projection residual lies in \(\mathcal C^\perp\).

Consequently, consensus-subspace language and projection fixed-point language describe the same nonanticipativity restriction, while the residual \((I-P_{\mathcal C})x\) measures its disagreement component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario vector is in consensus exactly when consensus projection leaves it unchanged; the projection residual is its orthogonal disagreement component.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Nonanticipativity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-indexed decisions with equality constraints on indistinguishable histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\) be a finite scenario set with stages \(t=1,\ldots,T\), and let \(h_t(\omega)\) denote the history observed through stage \(t\) under scenario \(\omega\). An explicit nonanticipative formulation introduces a separate decision \(x_t^\omega\) for each scenario and imposes \[x_t^\omega=x_t^{\omega'}\quad\text{whenever}\quad h_t(\omega)=h_t(\omega').\] Thus decisions may depend on information already observed, but not on scenario distinctions revealed after stage \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario-specific decisions are constrained to agree whenever their scenarios have identical histories at the decision stage.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) is finite and equipped with a staged information structure.
Each \(x_t^\omega\) lies in the same decision space for fixed \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_t(\omega)=h_t(\omega')\Longrightarrow x_t^\omega=x_t^{\omega'}\).

children.title: Implicit Nonanticipativity
children.top_down_role: Representations enforcing information consistency through shared indexing or structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Nonanticipativity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-indexed scenario-tree representation without separate equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal N_t\) be the information nodes at stage \(t\), and let \(n_t(\omega)\in\mathcal N_t\) be the unique node reached by scenario \(\omega\). Introduce one decision \(x_n\) for each node \(n\), and represent the scenario decision by \[x_t^\omega=x_{n_t(\omega)}.\] If two scenarios have the same observed history at stage \(t\), they reach the same node and therefore use the same decision automatically; no scenario-pair equality constraints are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One decision is attached to each information node, so scenarios sharing that node automatically share their decision.
assumptions_latex: The scenario tree represents exactly the staged information partition.
Each scenario reaches one information node at every stage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n_t(\omega)=n_t(\omega')\Longrightarrow x_t^\omega=x_t^{\omega'}\).

notation.meaning: stage-t node reached by scenario omega
decision associated with information node n

children.title: Dualized Nonanticipativity
children.top_down_role: Representations moving nonanticipativity into a dual coordination interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Dualized Nonanticipativity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian relaxation of linear nonanticipativity equations in a convex scenario formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the explicit nonanticipativity equations as \(Ax=0\), where \(x\) collects all scenario decision copies. For a separable objective \(F(x)=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p_\omega F_\omega(x^\omega)\) and product constraint set \(X=\prod_{\omega\in\Omega}X_\omega\), their Lagrangian relaxation is \[L(x,\lambda)=F(x)+\langle\lambda,Ax\rangle,\qquad d(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda).\] The dualized representation maximizes \(d(\lambda)\) over unrestricted multipliers \(\lambda\); for fixed \(\lambda\), the infimum decomposes by scenario when \(A\) is partitioned conformably.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonanticipativity equalities are moved into the objective with multipliers, producing scenario-separable subproblems and a Lagrangian dual bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Cartesian product of scenario constraint sets.
The objective and the columns of \(A\) are partitioned by scenario.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\lambda}d(\lambda)\leq\inf\{F(x):x\in X,\ Ax=0\}\).

notation.meaning: multiplier vector for the nonanticipativity equations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind fits and the weak-duality claim is plausible, but the decomposition and multiplier formulation require an authoritative, specifically located source.

children.title: Nonanticipativity Representation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural considerations governing selection among the three representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipativity Representation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence limits among explicit, implicit, and dualized representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Explicit equalities and information-node variables describe the same feasible policies when the node map identifies exactly those scenario-stage pairs having identical observed histories. This equivalence fails if the map merges distinguishable histories or separates indistinguishable histories. Dualization is different: for every multiplier it relaxes \(Ax=0\) and generally supplies only a lower bound for minimization. Equality with the nonanticipative primal value requires zero Lagrangian duality gap; recovery of a feasible optimal policy additionally requires primal attainment and enforcement, or limiting satisfaction, of \(Ax=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit and node-based forms are equivalent under an exact history partition; dualization is value-exact only under strong-duality and recovery conditions.
assumptions_latex: The explicit formulation uses equations \(Ax=0\).
The implicit formulation is defined by a scenario-tree node map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\mathrm{dual}}\leq v_{\mathrm{explicit}}=v_{\mathrm{implicit}}\), with the first equality only under zero duality gap.

notation.meaning: value of the explicit nonanticipative formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but equivalence under an exact history partition and the stated dual-value and policy-recovery boundaries lack cited support.

children.title: Fixed Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse regimes with scenario-invariant structural coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage linear recourse with a scenario-independent recourse matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the second-stage value function \[Q(x,\omega)=\inf_{y\geq0}\{q(\omega)^\top y:Wy=h(\omega)-T(\omega)x\}.\] The formulation has fixed recourse when the matrix \(W\) and the dimension and sign restrictions of \(y\) are independent of \(\omega\). The second-stage costs \(q(\omega)\), right-hand sides \(h(\omega)\), and technology matrices \(T(\omega)\) may remain scenario dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse is fixed when every scenario uses the same second-stage constraint matrix and recourse-variable structure.
assumptions_latex: The second-stage problem is linear and written in a common coordinate system.
All scenarios use recourse vectors of the same dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W(\omega)=W\) for every \(\omega\in\Omega\).

notation.meaning: second-stage optimal value after decision x in scenario omega

children.title: Variable Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse regimes permitting scenario-dependent structural coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage linear recourse whose recourse matrix varies by scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider second-stage problems written as \[Q(x,\omega)=\inf_{y\geq0}\{q(\omega)^\top y:W(\omega)y=h(\omega)-T(\omega)x\}.\] The formulation has variable recourse when the coefficient operator multiplying the recourse decision is scenario dependent: there is no single matrix \(W\) used for all scenarios in the specified common representation. Consequently, both the feasible recourse set and its dual feasible region may vary with \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse is variable when scenario realization changes the matrix multiplying the second-stage decision in the specified formulation.
assumptions_latex: The second-stage problems are linear and expressed in common recourse coordinates.
The scenario-dependent matrices have compatible row and column dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W(\omega)\) is not constant over \(\Omega\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit variable recourse in a common representation, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Recourse-Variability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Consequences of structural variability for scenario decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Variability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation-dependent boundary between fixed and variable recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fixed versus variable recourse is determined relative to a specified common representation. A model is fixed recourse precisely when all scenario matrices coincide in that representation. Scenario-dependent right-hand sides, costs, or technology matrices alone do not create variable recourse. Conversely, if \(W(\omega_1)\neq W(\omega_2)\), the displayed representation is variable recourse. This classification need not survive scenario-dependent changes of variables or constraint scaling: such transformations can transfer scenario dependence into or out of the recourse matrix, so representation equivalence does not imply classification invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only variation in the recourse matrix defines variable recourse, and scenario-dependent reformulations can change this representation-level classification.
assumptions_latex: All scenario subproblems are compared in one declared coordinate representation.
Scenario matrices have compatible dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{fixed recourse}\Longleftrightarrow (\exists W)(\forall\omega)\,W(\omega)=W\) in the declared representation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the claim that scenario-dependent transformations can move dependence into or out of the recourse matrix particularly requires sourced justification.

children.title: Complete Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse-feasibility regimes covering every relevant right-hand-side realization.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility of the recourse equations for every possible right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the linear recourse system \(Wy=r\), \(y\geq0\), the matrix \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has complete recourse if \[\{Wy:y\in\mathbb R_+^n\}=\mathbb R^m.\] Equivalently, for every right-hand side \(r\in\mathbb R^m\), there exists a nonnegative recourse action \(y\) satisfying \(Wy=r\). This property depends only on the recourse matrix and its recourse-variable cone, not on the distribution of realized right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete recourse means every right-hand side in the constraint space can be generated by a feasible nonnegative recourse action.
assumptions_latex: \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
Recourse decisions satisfy \(y\in\mathbb R_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W\mathbb R_+^n=\mathbb R^m\).

notation.meaning: cone generated by the columns of W

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cone-surjectivity definition is precise and appropriate for complete recourse, but no citation with a definition, section, or page locator is provided.

children.title: Relatively Complete Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse-feasibility regimes covering realizations induced by admissible first-stage choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Relatively Complete Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-sure recourse feasibility restricted to admissible first-stage decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the admissible first-stage set and let \(r(x,\omega)=h(\omega)-T(\omega)x\). A two-stage stochastic linear program has relatively complete recourse if \[\forall x\in X,\qquad \mathbb P\!\left(\{\omega:\exists y\geq0,\ Wy=r(x,\omega)\}\right)=1.\] Thus every admissible first-stage decision admits feasible recourse for almost every realized scenario, although \(Wy=r\), \(y\geq0\), may be infeasible for right-hand sides that cannot arise from admissible decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every admissible first-stage decision has feasible second-stage correction almost surely, though arbitrary right-hand sides need not be feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the declared admissible first-stage set.
The random data are measurable and the recourse system is well defined almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x\in X,\ \mathbb P(r(x,\omega)\in W\mathbb R_+^n)=1\).

notation.meaning: set of right-hand sides feasible under nonnegative recourse

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent under an almost-sure convention, but sources differ between almost-sure and support-wise formulations; a specific authoritative citation is required.

children.title: Incomplete Recourse
children.top_down_role: Regimes where some admissible first-stage choices lack feasible recourse.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of almost-sure recourse feasibility for some admissible first-stage decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the admissible first-stage set and \(r(x,\omega)=h(\omega)-T(\omega)x\). The model has incomplete recourse when relatively complete recourse fails; equivalently, \[\exists x\in X:\quad \mathbb P\!\left(r(x,\omega)\notin W\mathbb R_+^n\right)>0.\] For such a first-stage decision, the second-stage feasibility system \(Wy=r(x,\omega)\), \(y\geq0\), is infeasible on a set of scenarios having positive probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse is incomplete when some admissible first-stage decision produces an infeasible second-stage problem with positive probability.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the declared admissible first-stage set.
The random recourse right-hand side is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x\in X:\mathbb P(r(x,\omega)\notin W\mathbb R_+^n)>0\).

notation.meaning: set of right-hand sides admitting nonnegative recourse

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the logical failure of the record's almost-sure relative-completeness definition and fits the leaf, but that convention and terminology are uncited.

children.title: Recourse-Feasibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Decomposition consequences arising at transitions between recourse-feasibility regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Feasibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict distinction between complete and relatively complete recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Complete recourse implies relatively complete recourse for every admissible set and every realized right-hand side. The converse fails. For example, take scalar \(W=[1]\), \(y\geq0\), and suppose \(r(x,\omega)\geq0\) almost surely for every \(x\in X\). Then \(y=r(x,\omega)\) establishes relatively complete recourse. Complete recourse nevertheless fails because no \(y\geq0\) satisfies \(y=r\) for any \(r<0\). Incomplete recourse begins exactly when some admissible \(x\) yields an infeasible right-hand side with positive probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete recourse is stronger than relative completeness; the latter only covers right-hand sides reachable from admissible decisions almost surely.
assumptions_latex: Recourse feasibility is represented by \(Wy=r\), \(y\geq0\).
Relative feasibility is evaluated over the declared admissible set \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{complete}\Longrightarrow\text{relatively complete}\), but \(\text{relatively complete}\not\Longrightarrow\text{complete}\).

notation.meaning: right-hand side generated by decision x and scenario omega

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary classification and scalar counterexample are mathematically consistent, but the distinction and terminology lack an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Simple Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse structures with separable corrective components.

knowledge_statements.title: Simple Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable surplus-shortage correction with identity recourse blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear model has simple recourse when each random balance residual is corrected independently by nonnegative surplus and shortage variables. In canonical form, \[y^+-y^-=h(\omega)-T(\omega)x,\qquad y^+,y^-\geq0,\] with second-stage cost \(q_+(\omega)^\top y^++q_-(\omega)^\top y^-\), where the penalty vectors are componentwise nonnegative. The recourse matrix is \(W=[I,-I]\), so every finite residual has a feasible correction and the model has complete recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple recourse corrects each balance independently using nonnegative surplus and shortage variables, with separate linear penalties.
assumptions_latex: Residuals and recourse variables have the same finite dimension.
The surplus and shortage penalty vectors are componentwise nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W=[I,-I]\) and \(W\mathbb R_+^{2m}=\mathbb R^m\).

notation.meaning: identity matrix in the residual space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The canonical identity-block formulation and complete-recourse conclusion fit simple recourse, but the surplus/shortage sign convention and definition require a specifically located source.

children.title: Network Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse structures organized by network flow or related topology.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-recourse, two-stage linear model whose second-stage constraint matrix has network structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scenario \(s\), define \(Q_s(x)=\min\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y:Wy=h_s-T_sx,\ 0\le y\le u_s\}\). The model has network recourse when, after deleting one redundant row from each connected component and possibly multiplying rows or columns by \(-1\), the matrix \(W\) is a node-arc incidence matrix. Thus every column of \(W\) has at most one entry \(+1\), at most one entry \(-1\), and all other entries zero. The scenario subproblem is consequently a capacitated minimum-cost network-flow problem whenever its right-hand side is balanced and feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network recourse occurs when each linear recourse problem is a minimum-cost flow problem represented by a node-arc incidence matrix and scenario-dependent supplies.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and the second-stage variables are continuous.
\(W\), variable bounds, and dimensions are fixed across scenarios.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_s(x)\) is the value of a capacitated minimum-cost network-flow problem.

notation.meaning: scenario-s recourse value at first-stage decision x

REQUEST_SOURCES: authoritative stochastic-programming or network-recourse reference required.

children.title: General Polyhedral Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse structures represented by general polyhedral subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: General Polyhedral Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous linear recourse without simple- or network-matrix restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each scenario \(s\), general polyhedral recourse is the value function \[Q_s(x)=\inf\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y:W_sy=h_s-T_sx,\ y\ge0\},\] where \(W_s\) is an arbitrary finite real matrix of compatible dimensions. No separability, diagonal form, incidence structure, or total-unimodularity condition is imposed. For every \(x\) at which the subproblem is feasible and has finite value, linear-programming duality gives \[Q_s(x)=\max\{\pi^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx):W_s^{\mathsf T}\pi\le q_s\}.\] Hence \(Q_s\) is a polyhedral convex function on its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General polyhedral recourse is an arbitrary continuous linear second-stage problem; its dual representation makes the finite recourse value polyhedral and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(W_s\in\mathbb R^{m_s\times r_s}\), \(q_s\in\mathbb R^{r_s}\), and \(y\in\mathbb R_+^{r_s}\).
The recourse problem is feasible and has finite value at the stated \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_s\) admits the displayed dual representation and is polyhedral convex on \(\operatorname{dom}Q_s\).

notation.meaning: dual multiplier for the recourse equality
set of first-stage points with finite recourse value

review_flags: Supplied locators cover general linear programming but not this stochastic-recourse formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits General Polyhedral Recourse, and the primal-dual formulas are standard for finite continuous linear recourse. However, no cited source supports this stochastic-recourse formulation or the asserted polyhedral-convex value-function property.

children.title: Recourse-Structure Transitions
children.top_down_role: Navigation across increasing structural generality in recourse subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Structure Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of relaxing specialized recourse-matrix structure while retaining continuous linear recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(Q_s(x)=\inf\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y:W_sy=h_s-T_sx,\ y\ge0\}\). Replacing a simple- or network-structured matrix \(W_s\) by an arbitrary matrix moves the model into general polyhedral recourse. Whenever feasibility and finite value are preserved, the dual formula \[Q_s(x)=\max_{\pi}\{\pi^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx):W_s^{\mathsf T}\pi\le q_s\}\] and polyhedral convexity remain valid. What is lost is the specialized separable or network-flow representation: algorithms relying on diagonal blocks, incidence columns, or network-flow integrality are applicable only while those matrix predicates hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing simple or network matrix structure preserves the continuous LP dual representation, but removes the corresponding separable or network-flow specialization.
assumptions_latex: The second-stage variables remain continuous and nonnegative.
For the evaluated \(x\), each recourse problem is feasible with finite value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Generalization of \(W_s\) preserves polyhedral LP recourse but need not preserve specialized simple- or network-recourse structure.

notation.meaning: scenario recourse matrix undergoing structural change

review_flags: No supplied source locator treats transitions among simple, network, and general polyhedral recourse.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is locally appropriate for Recourse-Structure Transitions and distinguishes structural specialization from the underlying continuous LP representation. No source or locator supports the comparative claims concerning simple, network, and general polyhedral recourse.

children.title: Continuous Recourse
children.top_down_role: Continuous second-stage structure within scenario decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality regime in which every second-stage decision variable is real-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A two-stage model has continuous recourse when, for every scenario \(s\) and first-stage decision \(x\), its second-stage value is \[Q_s(x)=\inf\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y:W_sy=h_s-T_sx,\ y\in\mathbb R_+^{r_s}\}.\] Thus no component of \(y\) is restricted to an integer lattice. If the problem is feasible and bounded, its linear-programming dual is exact; consequently \(Q_s\) is polyhedral convex on its effective domain and can be supported by affine functions obtained from dual-feasible multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous recourse permits all second-stage decisions to be real-valued, yielding an LP value function with affine dual supports.
assumptions_latex: All second-stage constraints and costs are linear.
The recourse problem is feasible and bounded at the evaluated \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in\mathbb R_+^{r_s}\), and \(Q_s\) is a polyhedral convex LP value function on its effective domain.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically addresses continuous stochastic recourse.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Continuous Recourse leaf. The stronger conclusion that the entire value function is polyhedral convex and admits affine dual supports requires precise feasibility, properness, and boundedness conditions beyond a condition stated only at the evaluated point. A recourse-specific authoritative source is needed to settle the intended hypotheses.

children.title: Integer Recourse
children.top_down_role: Discrete second-stage structure within scenario decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality regime in which designated second-stage decisions lie on an integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A two-stage model has integer recourse when, for every scenario \(s\), its second-stage value has the form \[Q_s(x)=\inf\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y:W_sy=h_s-T_sx,\ y\in Y_s\cap\mathbb Z^{r_s}\},\] where \(Y_s\subseteq\mathbb R^{r_s}\) is a polyhedron. The lattice restriction is part of the recourse definition, not merely an algorithmic device. Unlike continuous linear recourse, the ordinary LP dual generally describes only the relaxation, so its affine dual functions are lower bounds and need not represent \(Q_s\) exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer recourse restricts second-stage decisions to lattice points; LP dual cuts then describe the relaxation and may not equal the true recourse value.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_s\) is a polyhedron and \(q_s^{\mathsf T}y\) is linear.
The integer feasible set is nonempty and has finite infimum at the evaluated \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_s\) is an integer-program value function, and LP-dual equality is not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: continuous polyhedral constraints of scenario s

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports integer recourse or its LP-relaxation boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and certificate boundary fit Integer Recourse: the ordinary LP dual generally represents only the continuous relaxation. No cited source or locator supports either the integer-recourse formulation or the LP-relaxation qualification.

children.title: Mixed Recourse Transitions
children.top_down_role: Structural boundaries between continuous, integer, or mixed recourse.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Recourse Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between continuous and partly integral second-stage value functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}\) index recourse variables constrained to be integral, and define \[Q_I(b)=\min\{q^{\mathsf T}y:Wy=b,\ y\ge0,\ y_i\in\mathbb Z\text{ for }i\in I\}.\] The transition \(I=\varnothing\) gives continuous recourse, while \(I\ne\varnothing\) gives mixed-integer recourse. Relaxing integrality produces \(Q_{\varnothing}(b)\le Q_I(b)\), with equality only when the relaxation has an optimal solution integral on \(I\). Concretely, \(\min\{y:y\ge b,\ y\in\mathbb Z_+\}=\lceil\max\{0,b\}\rceil\), whereas its continuous relaxation equals \(\max\{0,b\}\); thus convex polyhedral recourse is lost in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding even one integer recourse variable can create a relaxation gap and a discontinuous, nonconvex value function; equality survives when an integral relaxation optimum exists.
assumptions_latex: \(q\), \(W\), and \(b\) have compatible finite dimensions.
Both the mixed-integer problem and its continuous relaxation have finite optimal values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\varnothing}(b)\le Q_I(b)\), and strict inequality and loss of convexity can occur when \(I\ne\varnothing\).
review_flags: The concrete transition example is standard but unsupported by the supplied locators.
REQUEST_SOURCES: mixed-integer recourse value-function reference required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits Mixed Recourse Transitions, and the scalar ceiling example correctly exhibits a possible integrality gap and loss of convex polyhedral behavior. The transition claim and example have no supporting source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Stage Linear L-Shaped Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-scenario L-shaped method for continuous two-stage linear recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given probabilities \(p_s>0\), initialize a master containing \(x\in X\) and recourse surrogate \(\theta\). At iteration \(k\), minimize \(c^{\mathsf T}x+\theta\) subject to accumulated cuts, obtaining \(x^k\). For each scenario solve \[Q_s(x^k)=\min\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y:W_sy=h_s-T_sx^k,\ y\ge0\}.\] If a subproblem is infeasible, add a valid Farkas feasibility cut. Otherwise obtain an optimal dual vector \(\pi_s^k\) and add \[\theta\ge\sum_s p_s(\pi_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx).\] Stop when all subproblems are feasible and the incumbent objective minus the master lower bound is at most the prescribed tolerance; output the best incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The L-shaped method alternates between a first-stage master and scenario LPs, adding feasibility or dual optimality cuts until the upper-lower bound gap is small.
assumptions_latex: The scenario set is finite and \(p_s>0\) with \(\sum_s p_s=1\).
\(X\) is a nonempty polyhedron and all second-stage variables are continuous.
Every feasible recourse subproblem has finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, the returned incumbent has objective gap at most the prescribed tolerance relative to the master lower bound.

notation.meaning: optimal scenario dual multiplier at iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse Feasibility-Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas certificates excluding first-stage points with infeasible linear recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scenario \(s\), consider feasibility of \(W_sy=h_s-T_sx\) with \(y\ge0\). Define the alternative cone \(D_s=\{r:W_s^{\mathsf T}r\le0\}\). The recourse system is feasible if and only if \(r^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\le0\) for every \(r\in D_s\). Hence any ray \(r\in D_s\) satisfying \(r^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_s\bar x)>0\) certifies infeasibility at \(\bar x\), and the inequality \[r^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\le0\] is a valid feasibility cut. Extreme rays suffice to describe the entire cut family when \(D_s\) is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Farkas ray with positive pairing against the recourse right-hand side certifies infeasibility and yields a valid first-stage feasibility cut.
assumptions_latex: \(W_s\), \(h_s\), and \(T_s\) are finite-dimensional real data.
The recourse feasibility system is \(W_sy=h_s-T_sx\), \(y\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every violating \(r\in D_s\) yields the valid cut \(r^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\le0\).

notation.meaning: Farkas alternative cone for scenario s
first-stage point whose recourse is tested

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse Optimality-Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual affine lower supports for finite continuous linear recourse values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For feasible scenario recourse \[Q_s(x)=\min\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y:W_sy=h_s-T_sx,\ y\ge0\},\] let \(P_s=\{\pi:W_s^{\mathsf T}\pi\le q_s\}\). Every \(\pi\in P_s\) certifies the lower bound \(Q_s(x)\ge\pi^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\). Therefore \[\theta_s\ge\pi^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\] is a valid scenario optimality cut. For probabilities \(p_s\), any selection \(\pi_s\in P_s\) yields the aggregate cut \[\theta\ge\sum_s p_s\pi_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx).\] An optimal dual multiplier makes its scenario cut exact at the point where it was generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each dual-feasible multiplier gives an affine lower bound on recourse; optimal multipliers generate cuts touching the recourse value at the current point.
assumptions_latex: The recourse variables are continuous and nonnegative.
The scenario recourse problem is feasible and has finite value.
Scenario probabilities satisfy \(p_s\ge0\) and \(\sum_s p_s=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual-feasible multipliers produce valid scenario or aggregate optimality cuts, with equality at a generation point for optimal multipliers.

children.title: Single-Cut L-Shaped
children.top_down_role: Fully aggregated recourse certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Cut L-Shaped
knowledge_statements.scope_note: L-shaped variant adding one probability-weighted aggregate optimality cut per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Use one master variable \(\theta\) for expected recourse. At iteration \(k\), solve every feasible scenario subproblem at \(x^k\) and obtain optimal dual multipliers \(\pi_s^k\). Add the single aggregate inequality \[\theta\ge\sum_{s=1}^S p_s(\pi_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx).\] Feasibility cuts remain scenario-specific whenever recourse is infeasible. Reoptimize the master, and stop when all recourse systems are feasible and the incumbent upper bound differs from the master lower bound by at most the chosen tolerance. The master contains one expected-recourse epigraph variable regardless of the number of scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Single-cut L-shaped combines all scenario dual supports into one probability-weighted optimality cut at each iteration and uses one expected-recourse variable.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many scenarios with \(p_s>0\) and \(\sum_s p_s=1\).
All feasible recourse subproblems are continuous linear programs with finite optima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration contributes one aggregate optimality cut for expected recourse.

notation.meaning: scenario-s optimal dual multiplier at iteration k

children.title: Multicut L-Shaped

knowledge_statements.title: Multicut L-Shaped
knowledge_statements.scope_note: L-shaped variant maintaining a separate recourse surrogate and cuts for each scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Introduce master variables \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_S\) and minimize \(c^{\mathsf T}x+\sum_{s=1}^S p_s\theta_s\). At iteration \(k\), solve each scenario subproblem at \(x^k\). For every feasible scenario with optimal dual multiplier \(\pi_s^k\), add \[\theta_s\ge(\pi_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx).\] Add a scenario feasibility cut instead when recourse is infeasible. Reoptimize and stop when all scenarios are feasible and the incumbent upper bound minus the master lower bound is within tolerance. Thus as many as \(S\) optimality cuts are generated per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multicut L-shaped keeps one recourse variable per scenario and adds separate scenario optimality cuts, often strengthening the master at the cost of greater size.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many scenarios with \(p_s>0\) and \(\sum_s p_s=1\).
All feasible recourse subproblems are continuous linear programs with finite optima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration may add one distinct optimality cut for every scenario.

notation.meaning: scenario-s optimal dual multiplier at iteration k

children.title: Aggregation-Granularity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Computational consequences of choosing either aggregation extreme.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation-Granularity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Master-strength and size comparison for synchronized single cuts versus scenario-wise multicuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each scenario \(s\), let \(\Pi_s^K=\{\pi_s^1,\ldots,\pi_s^K\}\) be generated dual multipliers. The multicut master imposes every inequality \(\theta_s\ge\pi^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\) for \(\pi\in\Pi_s^K\), whereas the synchronized single-cut master imposes only \[\theta\ge\sum_s p_s(\pi_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx),\qquad k=1,\ldots,K.\] After identifying \(\theta=\sum_s p_s\theta_s\), every multicut-feasible master point satisfies every synchronized aggregate cut. Hence the multicut lower bound is at least the single-cut lower bound for the same generated multipliers, but it uses \(S\) epigraph variables and up to \(SK\) optimality constraints rather than one variable and \(K\) constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For identical generated multipliers, multicuts give a no-weaker master bound, while single cuts use fewer variables and constraints.
assumptions_latex: The two masters use the same first-stage region and generated multiplier vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_K^{\mathrm{multi}}\ge L_K^{\mathrm{single}}\), while the multicut master can be larger by a factor proportional to the scenario count.

notation.meaning: scenario-s dual multipliers generated through iteration K

children.title: Bunched L-Shaped
children.top_down_role: Certificate aggregation through fixed or adaptive scenario bunches.

knowledge_statements.title: Bunched L-Shaped
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition-based aggregation of optimality cuts for a finite-scenario two-stage stochastic linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), scenario probabilities \(p_s>0\), and convex polyhedral recourse functions \(Q_s\) be given. Choose a partition \(\mathcal B\) of the scenario set and initialize a master containing \(x\in X\) and variables \(\theta_B\). At iteration \(k\), solve the master, obtaining \(x^k\); for every scenario compute \(Q_s(x^k)\) and a subgradient \(g_s^k\in\partial Q_s(x^k)\). For each bunch \(B\in\mathcal B\), add
\[\theta_B\geq\sum_{s\in B}p_s\bigl(Q_s(x^k)+(g_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(x-x^k)\bigr).\]
The master minimizes \(c^{\mathsf T}x+\sum_{B\in\mathcal B}\theta_B\). Stop when its lower bound and the evaluated incumbent objective differ by at most the prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenarios are partitioned into bunches, and one probability-weighted supporting cut is added per bunch until the master and incumbent bounds agree sufficiently.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty and polyhedral.
Each \(Q_s\) is finite at every evaluated point and admits a computable subgradient.
The scenario set is finite and \(p_s>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each generated bunch inequality is a valid lower estimator of \(\sum_{s\in B}p_sQ_s(x)\).

notation.meaning: partition of scenarios into nonempty bunches
master epigraph variable for bunch B

children.title: Partially Aggregated L-Shaped
children.top_down_role: Intermediate aggregation between global cuts or scenario cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Partially Aggregated L-Shaped
knowledge_statements.scope_note: L-shaped method allowing simultaneous multicut and aggregated-cut blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite scenario set \(S\), select a partition \(\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots,P_m\}\), where singleton blocks represent disaggregated scenarios. The master minimizes \(c^{\mathsf T}x+\sum_{P\in\mathcal P}\theta_P\) over \(x\in X\). After obtaining \(x^k\), compute \(Q_s(x^k)\) and \(g_s^k\in\partial Q_s(x^k)\) for every \(s\). Add, for each block,
\[\theta_P\geq\sum_{s\in P}p_s\bigl(Q_s(x^k)+(g_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(x-x^k)\bigr).\]
Evaluate the full objective to update an incumbent and terminate at the requested bound gap. The all-singleton and one-block partitions recover the multicut and fully aggregated L-shaped masters, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario partition determines which recourse cuts remain separate and which are aggregated; its extreme partitions recover multicut and single-cut L-shaped methods.
assumptions_latex: The scenario set is finite with positive probabilities.
Every recourse function \(Q_s\) is convex and subdifferentiable at queried points.
The master is solved to the accuracy used in the stopping test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every block cut underestimates its block recourse function, so the master objective remains a valid lower bound.

notation.meaning: scenario recourse subgradient at iteration k

children.title: Scenario-Bunch Design
children.top_down_role: Structural choices governing scenario membership in cut groups.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite and \(p_s>0\) with \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\).
Each affine scenario cut globally underestimates \(Q_s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The summed bunch epigraph terms give a valid lower estimator of \(\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and coverage conditions for scenario groups used by bunched L-shaped cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A scenario-bunch design for finite \(S\) is a family \(\mathcal B=\{B_1,\ldots,B_m\}\) satisfying
\[B_i\neq\varnothing,\qquad B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\ (i\neq j),\qquad \bigcup_{i=1}^mB_i=S.\]
For each \(B\), its cut must use the same weights as the stochastic objective: if \(Q_s(x)\geq a_s^{\mathsf T}x+b_s\) for every \(s\in B\), then the bunch cut is
\[\theta_B\geq\sum_{s\in B}p_s(a_s^{\mathsf T}x+b_s).\]
Thus every scenario is counted exactly once. Any regrouping between iterations must replace, deactivate, or consistently reinterpret old block epigraph variables so that neither probability mass nor existing lower estimators are double-counted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid bunches partition the scenarios, preserve objective probabilities in their cuts, and handle regrouping without omitting or double-counting scenario mass.

children.title: Regularized L-Shaped Variants
children.top_down_role: Regularization interfaces for controlling master-problem movement.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized L-Shaped Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal stabilization of finite-scenario L-shaped master iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_k(x)\) be the current polyhedral L-shaped lower model of the objective \(F\) on a closed convex set \(X\). Given a center \(z^k\in X\) and \(\rho_k>0\), compute
\[x^k\in\arg\min_{x\in X}\left\{M_k(x)+\frac{\rho_k}{2}\lVert x-z^k\rVert^2\right\}.\]
Evaluate the scenario recourse functions at \(x^k\), append their valid supporting cuts to form \(M_{k+1}\), and compare actual objective decrease with model-predicted decrease. On a serious step set \(z^{k+1}=x^k\); otherwise retain \(z^{k+1}=z^k\). Stop when the incumbent upper bound minus the unregularized model lower bound is within tolerance. The proximal term selects trial points but is excluded from the reported stochastic-program lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal term stabilizes master trial points; serious-step logic updates the center, while certification uses the unregularized master lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex on nonempty closed convex \(X\).
\(M_k\leq F\) and new cuts are valid global minorants.
Regularization parameters remain positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method preserves valid L-shaped bounds while damping unstable movement of successive trial points.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but no specialized source establishes this particular proximal L-shaped variant, its serious-step policy, or the asserted lower-bound implementation. Different regularized decomposition methods use materially different stabilization and certification rules.

children.title: Inexact L-Shaped Variants
children.top_down_role: Controlled subproblem or master inexactness.

assumptions_latex: The exact objective is proper, closed, and convex.
The relevant objective level set is nonempty and bounded.
All displayed oracle and master error bounds are certified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Summable certified errors preserve asymptotic exactness of the cutting-plane model and its bound-gap test.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error conditions preserving asymptotic validity of inexact L-shaped cuts and master solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iteration \(k\), suppose the computed recourse affine function \(\ell_k\) satisfies
\[Q(x)\geq \ell_k(x)-\varepsilon_k\quad\text{for all }x\in X,\qquad Q(x^k)-\ell_k(x^k)\leq\varepsilon_k,\]
and the master trial point has optimization residual at most \(\delta_k\). A sufficient accuracy regime for an inexact L-shaped method is
\[\varepsilon_k\geq0,\quad\delta_k\geq0,\quad\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(\varepsilon_k+\delta_k)<\infty.\]
The master must include the corrected valid cut \(\theta\geq\ell_k(x)-\varepsilon_k\), and the stopping test must add certified remaining oracle and master errors to the nominal bound gap. Under the usual bounded-level-set assumption, these conditions prevent persistent computational error from invalidating convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact recourse and master errors are allowed when cuts are corrected, stopping bounds include residuals, and accumulated errors are summable.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact L-Shaped Variants

children.title: Parallel L-Shaped Variants
children.top_down_role: Concurrent scenario evaluation or certificate generation.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel L-Shaped Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous scenario-parallel evaluation with deterministic cut collection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite scenarios \(S\), solve the current L-shaped master to obtain \(x^k\), broadcast \(x^k\) to workers, and assign every \(s\in S\) to exactly one worker. In parallel, worker \(s\) solves its recourse problem and returns either an optimality-cut pair \((Q_s(x^k),g_s^k)\) or a valid feasibility cut. After a synchronization barrier, collect all required responses, add the corresponding single-scenario or prescribed aggregate cuts, update the incumbent using \(c^{\mathsf T}x^k+\sum_sp_sQ_s(x^k)\) when feasible, and solve the next master. Stop when the synchronized certified upper and lower bounds differ by at most tolerance. Exact parallel evaluation changes execution order, not the mathematical master sequence for a fixed cut policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario subproblems are evaluated concurrently, then their valid cuts and objective values are synchronized before the next master solve and bound test.
assumptions_latex: Scenario subproblems are conditionally independent once \(x^k\) is fixed.
Workers return exact solutions or certified errors handled by the cut policy.
Each synchronous iteration incorporates every required scenario response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed trial points and aggregation policy, synchronous parallel cut generation is mathematically equivalent to serial generation of the same cuts.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits and synchronous evaluation plausibly reproduces serial cut collection under a fixed policy. No cited source, however, supports the specialized parallel L-shaped procedure or the claimed equivalence; the generic parallel-computing inventory is insufficient.

children.title: Combined Variant Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility boundaries among regularization, inexactness, or parallel execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Variant Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient compatibility conditions for combining regularization, inexact solves, aggregation, and parallel evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A combined L-shaped implementation is bound-compatible if: (i) every aggregated or worker-generated cut, after any error correction, is a global minorant of the corresponding probability-weighted recourse term; (ii) the reported lower bound is obtained from the unregularized master, not from its proximal trial-point objective; (iii) every scenario is represented exactly once under the active aggregation design; and (iv) certified oracle and master residuals are included in stopping bounds and vanish, for example by summability. If asynchronous responses are permitted, a cut must be valid globally despite being generated at an earlier trial point, and no scenario may be postponed indefinitely. Under these conditions, parallelism and regularization alter trial-point production without compromising the common upper-lower certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variants are compatible when cuts remain globally valid, probabilities are counted once, regularization is excluded from lower bounds, and computational errors vanish and enter certification.
assumptions_latex: The underlying stochastic objective is proper, closed, and convex.
All cut corrections and residual bounds are computable.
Any asynchronous schedule has bounded delay or an equivalent fairness guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The combined method retains valid lower and upper bounds and an asymptotically exact termination gap.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the compatibility container, but the conclusion combines aggregation, regularization, inexactness, and asynchronous execution into a convergence and certification claim without a source. Fairness or bounded delay alone may not supply all assumptions needed for an asymptotically exact gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Scenario Nonanticipativity Duals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex finite-scenario dualization of equality among scenario copies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be finite, \(p_s>0\) with \(\sum_sp_s=1\), and let each \(F_s:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex. The nonanticipative primal problem is
\[v_P=\inf_{x_s=z}\sum_{s\in S}p_sF_s(x_s).\]
Using multipliers \(\lambda_s\) scaled by \(p_s\), its dual is
\[v_D=\sup_{\sum_sp_s\lambda_s=0}\sum_{s\in S}p_s\inf_{x_s}\bigl(F_s(x_s)+\lambda_s^{\mathsf T}x_s\bigr).\]
Weak duality gives \(v_D\leq v_P\). If a standard convex qualification holds, such as a common point in \(\bigcap_s\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}F_s)\), then \(v_D=v_P\) and, when attained, primal-dual optimizers satisfy the scenario stationarity and consensus conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing equality of scenario decisions yields separable scenario infima coordinated by multipliers whose probability-weighted sum is zero; a relative-interior condition gives strong duality.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite and all probabilities are positive.
Each \(F_s\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\bigcap_s\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}F_s)\neq\varnothing\) for strong duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_D\leq v_P\), and under the stated qualification \(v_D=v_P\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality role fits and the finite-scenario formulas are consistent with the stated probability-scaled multiplier convention. No source is cited for the exact formulation or relative-interior strong-duality qualification; the generic duality inventory does not specifically support this claim.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Distribution Nonanticipativity Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional-analytic nonanticipativity duality over a general probability space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), let \(\mathcal X=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\), let \(\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal X\) be the closed linear subspace of decisions measurable with respect to the prescribed information, and let \(I(x)=\mathbb E[f(x(\omega),\omega)]\) be proper, closed, and convex. With conjugate exponent \(q\), define
\[\mathcal N^\perp=\{\lambda\in L^q:\mathbb E\langle\lambda,x\rangle=0\text{ for all }x\in\mathcal N\}.\]
Then
\[\inf_{x\in\mathcal N}I(x)\geq\sup_{\lambda\in\mathcal N^\perp}\mathbb E\!\left[\inf_{u\in\mathbb R^n}\{f(u,\omega)+\langle\lambda(\omega),u\rangle\}\right].\]
Equality holds when integral-conjugacy interchange is valid and a suitable continuity or relative-interior qualification holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For general distributions, nonanticipativity is a closed information subspace; its annihilator supplies dual multipliers, with strong duality requiring integral interchange and convex qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(1\leq p<\infty\) and \(q\) is its conjugate exponent.
\(f\) is a measurable normal convex integrand and \(I\) is proper and closed.
A continuity or relative-interior qualification holds for equality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The annihilator dual gives a lower bound, and equals the nonanticipative primal value under the stated interchange and qualification conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality role fits, but the strong-duality statement deliberately leaves the integral-interchange and continuity qualification unspecified. Those details depend on the function spaces, decomposability, normal-integrand hypotheses, and endpoint treatment, so an authoritative functional-analytic source is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Separable Dual Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected dual ascent coordinating independently solved finite-scenario subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For multipliers satisfying \(\sum_sp_s\lambda_s^0=0\), iteration \(k\) solves independently
\[x_s^k\in\arg\min_x\{F_s(x)+(\lambda_s^k)^{\mathsf T}x\},\qquad s\in S.\]
Form the weighted consensus point \(\bar x^k=\sum_sp_sx_s^k\) and update
\[\lambda_s^{k+1}=\lambda_s^k+\alpha_k(x_s^k-\bar x^k),\qquad \alpha_k>0.\]
Because \(\sum_sp_s(x_s^k-\bar x^k)=0\), dual feasibility is preserved. Record the separable dual value as a lower bound and stop only when a certified dual-primal gap or a prescribed consensus-and-stationarity test is met. For nonsmooth concave dual objectives, standard diminishing steps satisfy \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\) and \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario subproblems are solved independently, and their disagreement from the weighted consensus updates dual multipliers while preserving the zero-mean multiplier constraint.
assumptions_latex: Each scenario infimum is attained at every multiplier queried.
The scenario set is finite with positive probabilities.
For convergence, dual maximizers exist and subgradients are bounded on the iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update preserves \(\sum_sp_s\lambda_s^k=0\) and performs feasible subgradient ascent on the nonanticipativity dual.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits and the update preserves the weighted-zero multiplier constraint. A source is still required for the identification as projected subgradient ascent and for the convergence conditions attached to diminishing step sizes.

children.title: Nonanticipativity Dual Bounds
children.top_down_role: Dual-bound roles within scenario-separable coordination.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipativity Dual Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computable lower-bound certificate from feasible nonanticipativity multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the finite-scenario convex primal value
\[v_P=\inf_{x_s=z}\sum_sp_sF_s(x_s),\]
let \(\lambda=(\lambda_s)_{s\in S}\) satisfy \(\sum_sp_s\lambda_s=0\), and suppose certified numbers \(m_s\) obey
\[m_s\leq\inf_x\{F_s(x)+\lambda_s^{\mathsf T}x\}.\]
Then
\[L(\lambda)=\sum_sp_sm_s\leq v_P.\]
The certificate consists of the multiplier vector, verification of its weighted zero sum, and the scenario lower-bound certificates establishing each \(m_s\). Exact scenario minima may replace \(m_s\). The inequality requires neither dual attainment nor strong duality; those assumptions are needed only to assert that the best such bound reaches \(v_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted-zero multipliers plus certified lower bounds for all scenario Lagrangian subproblems provide a directly checkable lower bound on the nonanticipative optimum.
assumptions_latex: Each reported \(m_s\) is a certified lower bound for its scenario infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(\lambda)=\sum_sp_sm_s\leq v_P\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role exactly fits the terminal container, and the bound is a plausible weak-duality certificate under the stated scaling. Nevertheless, the candidate has no citation for the nonanticipativity Lagrangian construction or its certificate interpretation.

children.title: Implementable Primal Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of nonanticipative implementable decisions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, so the projection exists.
All scenario recourse feasibility and objective values can be certified.
The stochastic problem is a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted \(\hat x^k\) is nonanticipative and feasible, and its evaluated value \(U_k\) is a valid primal upper bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of a common feasible decision from scenario-dependent dual iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given scenario decisions \(x_s^k\), form \(y^k=\sum_s p_sx_s^k\) and compute a common decision
\[\hat x^k\in\arg\min_{x\in X}\frac12\lVert x-y^k\rVert^2.\]
Set every scenario copy to \(\hat x^k\), solve or evaluate all recourse problems at this common decision, and accept the candidate only if every deterministic and recourse constraint is certified feasible. Its value
\[U_k=c^{\mathsf T}\hat x^k+\sum_s p_sQ_s(\hat x^k)\]
is then an upper bound on the stochastic optimum; retain the best accepted value. Projection alone certifies first-stage consensus and membership in \(X\), but it does not certify recourse feasibility, which must be checked separately. Stop when the best recovered upper bound and a certified dual lower bound meet the chosen tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the weighted scenario decisions onto the common first-stage set, verify all recourse constraints, and use each accepted common decision as an upper-bound incumbent.
knowledge_statements.title: Implementable Primal Recovery

children.title: Dual-to-Primal Gap Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Relationship between dual evidence or recovered primal quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-to-Primal Gap Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality certificate for a finite convex scenario-consensus formulation and an implementable recovered decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be finite, let \(p_s>0\) with \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\), and let \(f_s\) be extended-real convex scenario objectives. Define \(P^*=\inf_z\sum_s p_s f_s(z)\). For multipliers satisfying \(\sum_s p_s\lambda_s=0\), define \(d(\lambda)=\sum_s p_s\inf_x\{f_s(x)+\langle\lambda_s,x\rangle\}\). If \(\widehat z\) is implementable and \(F(\widehat z)=\sum_s p_s f_s(\widehat z)<+\infty\), then \[d(\lambda)\le P^*\le F(\widehat z),\qquad 0\le F(\widehat z)-P^*\le F(\widehat z)-d(\lambda).\] Thus the computable dual-to-primal gap certifies an upper bound on primal suboptimality; a zero gap certifies primal and dual optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible recovered policy and a balanced dual point bracket the optimum; their objective gap bounds primal suboptimality, and a zero gap certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f_s\) is proper, closed, and convex for every \(s\in S\).
\(\widehat z\in\bigcap_s\operatorname{dom}f_s\).
\(\sum_s p_s\lambda_s=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le F(\widehat z)-P^*\le F(\widehat z)-d(\lambda)\).

notation.meaning: optimal value of the nonanticipative primal problem

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Stage Progressive Hedging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-scenario convex progressive hedging for two-stage first-stage consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\rho>0\), initialize scenario decisions \(x_s^0\), set \(z^0=\sum_s p_sx_s^0\), and choose \(\lambda_s^0\) with \(\sum_s p_s\lambda_s^0=0\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), compute in parallel \[x_s^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\left\{f_s(x)+\langle\lambda_s^k,x\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x-z^k\rVert^2\right\},\] then set \(z^{k+1}=\sum_s p_sx_s^{k+1}\) and \(\lambda_s^{k+1}=\lambda_s^k+\rho(x_s^{k+1}-z^{k+1})\). Stop when \(\max_s\lVert x_s^{k+1}-z^{k+1}\rVert\le\varepsilon_{m pri}\) and \(\rho\lVert z^{k+1}-z^k\rVert\le\varepsilon_{m dual}\); return \(z^{k+1}\) with scenario recourse solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Progressive hedging alternates parallel penalized scenario solves, probability-weighted consensus averaging, and multiplier updates until primal and dual residuals are small.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite and \(p_s>0\) with \(\sum_s p_s=1\).
Each scenario subproblem attains its displayed minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}\) is the consensus iterate and \(\lambda_s^{k+1}\) penalizes scenario disagreement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario decomposition for a two-stage stochastic program using probability-weighted consensus and multiplier updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a nonanticipative \(x^0\), an initial multiplier \(\rho^0\), and \(r>0\). At iteration \(v\), solve the scenario subproblems to obtain \((x_k^{v+1},y_k^{v+1})\) for \(k=1,\ldots,K\). Define the replicated consensus vector by \(\widehat x^{v+1,k}=\sum_{l=1}^K p_lx^{v+1,l}\) for every \(k\), and update \(\rho_k^{v+1}=\rho_k^v+r(x_k^{v+1}-\widehat x^{v+1,k})\). If \(\widehat x^{v+1}=\widehat x^v\) and \(\rho^{v+1}=\rho^v\), stop; the fixed-point consensus and multiplier are optimal. Otherwise increment \(v\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Progressive hedging alternates independent scenario solves, probability-weighted averaging of first-stage decisions, and multiplier corrections proportional to each scenario's disagreement with consensus. An unchanged consensus and multiplier form the stated optimal stopping condition.
assumptions_latex: x^0\text{ is nonanticipative}
\rho^0\text{ is an initial multiplier}
p_l\geq0,\qquad \sum_{l=1}^Kp_l=1

knowledge_statements.title: Multistage Policy Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional scenario averaging that projects a multistage policy onto the nonanticipativity subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_t(s)\) denote the stage-\(t\) information node reached by scenario \(s\), and let \(x_{s,t}\) be its stage decision. For every node \(n\), define \(S(n)=\{s:h_t(s)=n\}\) and \(p(n)=\sum_{s\in S(n)}p_s\). The aggregated policy is \[z_{n,t}=\frac{1}{p(n)}\sum_{s\in S(n)}p_sx_{s,t},\qquad (P_{\mathcal N}x)_{s,t}=z_{h_t(s),t}.\] Hence \(P_{\mathcal N}\) is the orthogonal projection, under \(\langle x,y\rangle_p=\sum_{s,t}p_s\langle x_{s,t},y_{s,t}\rangle\), onto policies equal across scenarios sharing the same observed history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each scenario-tree node, probability-weighted averaging produces the closest policy whose decisions agree across scenarios with the same history.
assumptions_latex: The scenario tree and stagewise history map \(h_t\) are fixed.
Every reached node has \(p(n)>0\).
Scenario decisions lie in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathcal N}x\in\mathcal N\) and \(P_{\mathcal N}x\) is the weighted orthogonal projection of \(x\) onto \(\mathcal N\).

children.title: Convex Convergence Regime
children.top_down_role: Convex settings supporting progressive-hedging convergence claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Convergence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convergence of exact progressive hedging in the closed convex consensus regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each \(f_s:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and suppose the consensus problem \(\min_z\sum_s p_sf_s(z)\) has a primal-dual saddle point. Apply exact progressive hedging with fixed \(\rho>0\) and balanced initial multipliers. Then the primal residuals satisfy \(x_s^k-z^k\to0\), the consensus iterates converge to a primal solution \(z^*\), the objective values converge to the optimal value, and the multipliers converge to a dual solution. Consequently, every limiting scenario policy is nonanticipative and optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With closed convex scenario objectives, exact subproblem solves, a saddle point, and positive fixed penalty, progressive hedging converges to consensus optimality.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_s\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
A primal-dual saddle point exists.
Subproblems are solved exactly and \(\rho>0\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_s^k-z^k\to0\), \(z^k\to z^*\), and \(\sum_s p_sf_s(z^k)\to P^*\).

children.title: Convex Optimality Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT certificate for global optimality of a convex scenario-consensus decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a candidate \(z\in\bigcap_s\operatorname{dom}f_s\), suppose there exist multipliers \(\lambda_s\) and subgradients \(g_s\in\partial f_s(z)\) such that \[g_s+\lambda_s=0\quad\text{for every }s,\qquad \sum_s p_s\lambda_s=0.\] These conditions are finitely checkable from scenario subgradients and multiplier balance. Convex subgradient inequalities then imply that \(z\) globally minimizes \(\sum_s p_sf_s\). Equivalently, primal consensus feasibility, scenario stationarity, and dual balance form an exact convex optimality certificate; paired primal and dual values coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consensus feasibility, one subgradient stationarity equation per scenario, and balanced multipliers certify global optimality for convex scenario objectives.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_s\) is proper and convex.
\(z\in\bigcap_s\operatorname{dom}f_s\).
The displayed subgradients and multipliers are available for verification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\in\operatorname*{argmin}_u\sum_s p_sf_s(u)\) and the primal-dual gap is zero.

children.title: Certificate Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits beyond which convex certificates no longer apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity is essential when stationarity and consensus residuals are interpreted as global-optimality certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Remove convexity and consider the single-scenario objective \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) defined by \(f(x)=x^4-x^2\). At \(x=0\), the consensus residual is zero and \(f'(0)=0\), so a residual-plus-stationarity test accepts the point. Nevertheless, \(f(0)=0\), while \(f(1/\sqrt2)=f(-1/\sqrt2)=-1/4\). Thus zero consensus and stationarity residuals do not certify global optimality for nonconvex scenario problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity, zero consensus and stationarity residuals may hold at a point that is not globally optimal.
assumptions_latex: The convexity assumption is removed.
Stationarity is tested only by a zero derivative.
No separate global lower bound is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=0\) satisfies stationarity but is not globally optimal because \(f(0)=0>-1/4=f(1/\sqrt2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Parameter Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar, scenario-dependent, and operator-valued quadratic penalties for progressive-hedging subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A penalty-parameter variant assigns each scenario a self-adjoint positive-definite operator \(M_s\) and replaces the scalar penalty by \(\tfrac12\lVert x-z^k\rVert_{M_s}^2\), where \(\lVert v\rVert_{M_s}^2=\langle v,M_sv\rangle\). The scenario update is \[x_s^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\left\{f_s(x)+\langle\lambda_s^k,x\rangle+\frac12\lVert x-z^k\rVert_{M_s}^2\right\}.\] The classical variant has \(M_s=\rho I\); scenario-dependent scalar penalties have \(M_s=\rho_sI\). A uniformly coercive family satisfies \(mI\preceq M_s\preceq LI\) for constants \(0<m\le L<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Progressive hedging may use a common scalar, scenario-specific scalars, or positive-definite operator penalties, with uniform coercivity supporting stable metric-proximal updates.
assumptions_latex: Each \(M_s\) is self-adjoint.
The penalty family is positive definite.
Scenario subproblems attain their minima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_s=\rho I\), \(M_s=\rho_sI\), and uniformly coercive operator choices are penalty-parameter variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus-Metric Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted-metric projection formula for centralized progressive-hedging consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_s\succ0\) and equip scenario vectors with \(\langle x,y\rangle_{p,M}=\sum_s p_s\langle x_s,M_sy_s\rangle\). The metric projection onto the consensus subspace \(\mathcal N=\{x:x_s=z\text{ for some }z\}\) is \[(P_{\mathcal N}^{M}x)_s=z_M,\qquad z_M=\left(\sum_s p_sM_s\right)^{-1}\sum_s p_sM_sx_s.\] Thus Euclidean averaging, diagonal coordinate scaling, and full positive-definite preconditioning are consensus-metric variants obtained respectively from scalar, diagonal, and full choices of \(M_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The consensus point is a metric-weighted scenario average; scalar, diagonal, and full positive-definite metrics yield different projections onto the same consensus subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite and \(p_s>0\).
Every \(M_s\) is self-adjoint and positive definite.
All scenario decisions share the same finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathcal N}^{M}x\) is given by the displayed metric-weighted average.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Scaling Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent probability-weighted and unweighted conventions for scenario objectives, multipliers, and penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p_s>0\), the weighted scenario subproblem \[\operatorname*{argmin}_x\left\{p_sf_s(x)+\langle y_s,x\rangle+\frac{p_s\rho}{2}\lVert x-z\rVert^2\right\}\] has the same minimizers as \[\operatorname*{argmin}_x\left\{f_s(x)+\langle\lambda_s,x\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x-z\rVert^2\right\},\qquad \lambda_s=y_s/p_s.\] The compatible multiplier updates are \(y_s^+=y_s+p_s\rho(x_s^+-z^+)\) and \(\lambda_s^+=\lambda_s+\rho(x_s^+-z^+)\). Therefore probabilities may be placed inside scenario objectives or absorbed into dual variables, but all associated terms must be scaled consistently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Probability-weighted and unweighted scenario formulations are equivalent after rescaling multipliers and penalty updates consistently; partial rescaling changes the algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \(p_s>0\) for every scenario.
The same positive penalty \(\rho\) is used under both conventions.
Multipliers satisfy \(y_s=p_s\lambda_s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two displayed scenario subproblems have identical minimizer sets.
