children.title: Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Cost measured through calls to abstract separation or optimization oracles.

assumptions_latex: An oracle model and an accuracy certificate are fixed.
The instance class \(\mathcal F\) and permitted algorithm class \(\mathcal A\) are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The oracle complexity is \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{orc}}(\varepsilon)=\inf_{A
i\mathcal A}\sup_{P
i\mathcal F}N_{\mathrm{orc}}(A,P,\varepsilon)\), interpreted in the extended nonnegative integers.

notation.meaning: Number of oracle calls before certification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case deterministic query complexity under a declared decomposition oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance class \(\mathcal F\), an algorithm class \(\mathcal A\), an oracle that specifies each admissible query and response, and an \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy certificate. For algorithm \(A\) and instance \(P\), let \(N_{\mathrm{orc}}(A,P,\varepsilon)\) be the number of oracle calls made before \(A\) returns a valid certificate, with value \(+\infty\) if it never does. The worst-case oracle complexity is \[\mathcal C_{\mathrm{orc}}(\varepsilon)=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A}\sup_{P\in\mathcal F}N_{\mathrm{orc}}(A,P,\varepsilon).\] Arithmetic performed outside the oracle is excluded unless separately charged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle complexity is the smallest worst-case number of declared oracle calls needed to produce the required accuracy certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the selected deterministic minimax oracle model. The conclusion also uses A\ni\mathcal A and P\ni\mathcal F instead of A\in\mathcal A and P\in\mathcal F, contradicting the statement.

children.title: Pricing Complexity
children.top_down_role: Cost of detecting or producing improving columns.

assumptions_latex: A restricted master solution supplies dual multipliers \(y\).
Pricing returns a column minimizing reduced cost to tolerance \(\delta\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pricing complexity counts the resources required either to produce a column with reduced cost below \(-\delta\) or to certify that no such column exists.

notation.meaning: Reduced cost of a candidate column

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-call complexity of approximate reduced-cost pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given restricted-master multipliers \(y\), define the reduced cost of an admissible column \(j\in\mathcal J\) by \(\bar c(j;y)=c_j-a_j^{\mathsf T}y\). A \(\delta\)-accurate pricing call must either return \(j
i\mathcal J\) with \(\bar c(j;y)<-\delta\), or certify \(\inf_{j
i\mathcal J}\bar c(j;y)\geq-\delta\). Its pricing complexity \(C_{\mathrm{price}}(\delta)\) is the worst-case declared resource needed for this task over the chosen multiplier and instance classes. The resource may be operations, nodes, or time, but must be fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing complexity measures the worst-case work to find a sufficiently negative reduced-cost column or certify that none exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Pricing Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this pricing-complexity convention, and the statement twice uses j\ni\mathcal J where j\in\mathcal J is required.

children.title: Subproblem Complexity
children.top_down_role: Cost of solving decomposed local, block, or scenario problems.

assumptions_latex: The decomposition specifies a family of subproblems \(Q_s(z)\), indexed by \(s\), at master state \(z\).
A subproblem accuracy certificate with tolerance \(\delta\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Subproblem complexity is \(C_{\mathrm{sub}}(\delta)=\sup_{s,z}C_s(z,\delta)\) over the declared admissible index-state set.

notation.meaning: Resources needed for one certified solve

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case cost of one certified decomposition subproblem solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each admissible subproblem index \(s\) and master state \(z\), let \(C_s(z,\delta)\) be the declared computational resource required to return a \(\delta\)-accurate solution or an accepted infeasibility or unboundedness certificate for \(Q_s(z)\). The subproblem complexity is \[C_{\mathrm{sub}}(\delta)=\sup_{(s,z)\in\mathcal D}C_s(z,\delta),\] where \(\mathcal D\) is the specified index-state domain. For parallel execution, total work and critical-path depth are distinct measures and must be reported separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subproblem complexity is the worst-case declared resource needed for one certified subproblem solve over admissible blocks and master states.
knowledge_statements.title: Subproblem Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but no inspectable source supports the selected worst-case resource and certification model.

children.title: Nested-Oracle Cost
children.top_down_role: Total scaling when pricing or subproblem solution itself invokes inner oracles.

assumptions_latex: Oracle calls form a finite rooted call tree \(T\).
Each node \(v\) has local cost \(c_v\geq0\), excluding descendant work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
Sequential nested-oracle work equals \(C(T)=\sum_{v
i T}c_v\); for a level-regular tree this becomes \(C(T)=\sum_{\ell=0}^L(\prod_{h=0}^{\ell-1}b_h)c_{\ell}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential work accounting for a finite hierarchy of nested oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a nested computation by a finite rooted call tree \(T\), and assign each call node \(v\) a local cost \(c_v\) that excludes all descendant calls. The exact sequential work is \[C(T)=\sum_{v\in T}c_v.\] If every level-\(\ell\) call has local cost \(c_{\ell}\) and launches \(b_{\ell}\) children, then \[C(T)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\left(\prod_{h=0}^{\ell-1}b_h\right)c_{\ell},\] with the empty product equal to \(1\). This representation prevents descendant oracle costs from being counted both locally and recursively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested-oracle work is the sum of exclusive local costs over the call tree, or equivalently a levelwise branching-weighted sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Oracle Cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The call-tree representation is mathematically coherent, but it lacks a source. The conclusion also uses v\ni T instead of v\in T.

children.title: Cut Complexity
children.top_down_role: Scaling in the number, size, or management burden of generated cuts.

assumptions_latex: A cut-generating method has a declared termination certificate at accuracy \(\varepsilon\).
Only cuts actually inserted into the maintained relaxation are counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cut complexity is \(K_{\mathrm{cut}}(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal F}K(P,\varepsilon)\), with value \(+\infty\) when certified termination is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case number of inserted cuts before certified termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a problem class \(\mathcal F\), a cut-generation rule, an insertion policy, and an \(\varepsilon\)-termination certificate. For instance \(P\), let \(K(P,\varepsilon)\) be the number of cuts inserted into the maintained relaxation before the certificate is first satisfied; set it to \(+\infty\) if this never occurs. The cut complexity is \[K_{\mathrm{cut}}(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal F}K(P,\varepsilon).\] Rejected candidates, duplicate cuts, and deleted cuts are excluded unless the counting convention explicitly includes them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut complexity is the worst-case number of cuts inserted before a cutting method first obtains its declared accuracy certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the cut-complexity leaf, but no source supports the selected inserted-cut counting convention or worst-case formulation.

children.title: Column Complexity
children.top_down_role: Scaling in the number, size, or management burden of generated columns.

assumptions_latex: A column-generating method has a declared termination certificate at accuracy \(\varepsilon\).
Only columns actually inserted into the restricted master are counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The column complexity is \(K_{\mathrm{col}}(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal F}J(P,\varepsilon)\), with value \(+\infty\) if certified termination can fail.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case number of inserted columns before certified termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a problem class \(\mathcal F\), a pricing rule, a column-insertion policy, and an \(\varepsilon\)-termination certificate. For instance \(P\), let \(J(P,\varepsilon)\) be the number of columns inserted into the restricted master before the certificate is first satisfied; set it to \(+\infty\) if this never occurs. The column complexity is \[K_{\mathrm{col}}(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal F}J(P,\varepsilon).\] Generated but rejected columns, duplicates, and initial columns are excluded unless the declared counting convention includes them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Column complexity is the worst-case number of columns inserted before a column-generation method first achieves its declared certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Column Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the column-complexity leaf, but no source supports the selected inserted-column counting convention or worst-case formulation.

children.title: Iteration Complexity
children.top_down_role: Scaling in outer coordination or master-update rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic residual-based iteration complexity for a decomposition method with a certified rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r_k\ge 0\) be the certified residual after iteration \(k\), and define \(N(\varepsilon)=\inf\{k\in\mathbb N_0:r_k\le\varepsilon\}\). If constants \(C>0\) and \(q>0\) satisfy \(r_k\le C(k+1)^{-q}\) for every \(k\ge0\), then
\[
N(\varepsilon)\le \max\left\{0,\left\lceil(C/\varepsilon)^{1/q}\right\rceil-1\right\}.
\]
Thus the method has iteration complexity \(O(\varepsilon^{-1/q})\), where one iteration comprises one master update and its prescribed subproblem-generation phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual rate of order k to the negative q implies at most order epsilon to the negative 1/q decomposition iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(r_k\) is a valid termination certificate.
\(r_k\le C(k+1)^{-q}\) for constants \(C,q>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon^{-1/q})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional residual-to-iteration bound is mathematically correct and the complexity-bound kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the residual-rate framework or decomposition interpretation.

children.title: Generation–Iteration Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between richer generated batches and fewer outer rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Generation–Iteration Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint accounting of iterations and generated cuts, columns, or scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose iteration \(k\) generates \(g_k\in\mathbb N_0\) objects and reduces a certificate according to \(r_{k+1}\le \rho(g_k)r_k\), where \(\rho:\mathbb N_0\to(0,1]\) is nonincreasing. After \(K\) iterations,
\[
r_K\le r_0\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\rho(g_k),\qquad G_K=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}g_k.
\]
With coordination cost \(c_I\) per iteration and generation cost \(c_G\) per object, the generation–iteration tradeoff is represented by minimizing \(c_IK+c_GG_K\) subject to \(r_0\prod_k\rho(g_k)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generating more objects per iteration can reduce the required iterations, while total cost balances coordination against generation work.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho(g)\in(0,1]\) is nonincreasing in \(g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{c_IK+c_G\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}g_k:r_0\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\rho(g_k)\le\varepsilon\}\) represents the tradeoff.

notation.meaning: certificate contraction factor from generating g objects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is internally consistent and fits the tradeoff leaf, but the contraction and cost model is an uncited constructed abstraction.

children.title: Scenario Complexity
children.top_down_role: Scaling with the number or heterogeneity of modeled scenarios.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work growth under explicit enumeration of finite stochastic scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a finite-support stochastic program with scenarios \(s=1,\ldots,S\). If every decomposition iteration solves exactly one subproblem for every scenario and scenario \(s\) costs \(c_{k,s}\) operations at iteration \(k\), then after \(K\) iterations the scenario-subproblem work is
\[
W_{m scen}(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\sum_{s=1}^{S}c_{k,s}.
\]
If \(c_-\le c_{k,s}\le c_+\) uniformly for positive constants \(c_-\) and \(c_+\), then \(KSc_-\le W_{m scen}(K)\le KSc_+\), hence \(W_{m scen}(K)=\Theta(KS)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit scenario decomposition performs work linear in both the number of iterations and enumerated scenarios when subproblem costs are uniformly bounded.
assumptions_latex: All \(S\) scenario subproblems are processed at every iteration.
\(0<c_-\le c_{k,s}\le c_+<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_{m scen}(K)=\Theta(KS)\).

notation.meaning: work for scenario s at iteration k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated linear work accounting follows from its explicit assumptions and fits a complexity-bound container, but no stochastic-decomposition source is cited.

children.title: Sample Complexity
children.top_down_role: Statistical scaling associated with sampled uncertainty representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise Monte Carlo accuracy for a bounded stochastic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) be independent copies of a random variable \(Z\in[a,b]\) almost surely, and let \(\widehat\mu_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\) estimate \(\mu=\mathbb E[Z]\). For \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\),
\[
n\ge \frac{(b-a)^2}{2\varepsilon^2}\log\frac{2}{\delta}
\]
implies \(\mathbb P(|\widehat\mu_n-\mu|\le\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\). Thus pointwise bounded-loss estimation has sample complexity \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))\); this does not by itself give uniform optimization guarantees over a decision set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded expected value can be estimated within epsilon with confidence 1−delta using order epsilon⁻² log(1/delta) independent samples.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) are independent and identically distributed.
\(Z_i\in[a,b]\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(|\widehat\mu_n-\mu|\le\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is the standard pointwise Hoeffding bound and correctly disclaims uniform optimization guarantees, but it has no citation.

children.title: Scenario-Tree Complexity
children.top_down_role: Growth caused by multistage branching and history dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Tree Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node and leaf growth of a finite multistage scenario tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a rooted \(T\)-stage scenario tree with uniform branching factor \(b_t\ge1\) from stage \(t\) to \(t+1\), the number of stage-\(t\) nodes is \(n_t=\prod_{j=1}^{t-1}b_j\). Consequently,
\[
N_T=1+\sum_{t=2}^{T}\prod_{j=1}^{t-1}b_j,
\qquad
L_T=\prod_{j=1}^{T-1}b_j,
\]
where \(N_T\) and \(L_T\) are the total nodes and terminal scenarios. For constant \(b>1\), \(N_T=(b^T-1)/(b-1)\) and \(L_T=b^{T-1}\), so explicit tree storage and full traversal are exponential in the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multistage tree multiplies branches across stages; with constant branching above one, its nodes and terminal scenarios grow exponentially with horizon.
assumptions_latex: The tree has \(T\) stages.
Every stage-\(t\) node has exactly \(b_t\) children.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The node and leaf counts are correct for the stated stage-uniform branching model, and the content kind fits, but no scenario-tree source is supplied.

children.title: Tree-Reduction Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Computational versus representational consequences of reducing scenario trees.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Reduction Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-error control from Wasserstein scenario-tree reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be the original disturbance distribution and \(\widetilde P\) a reduced finite-tree distribution. Suppose \(Q(x,\xi)\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in \(\xi\), uniformly for \(x\in X\), under the metric defining \(W_1\). Then
\[
\sup_{x\in X}\left|\mathbb E_P Q(x,\xi)-\mathbb E_{\widetilde P}Q(x,\xi)\right|\le L W_1(P,\widetilde P).
\]
If both optimization problems attain finite minima \(v(P)\) and \(v(\widetilde P)\), then \(|v(P)-v(\widetilde P)|\le L W_1(P,\widetilde P)\). Reducing nodes lowers representation cost while the Wasserstein discrepancy controls worst-case objective distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree reduction lowers representation size, while a Lipschitz objective limits optimal-value error by the Wasserstein distance to the original distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(x,\cdot)\) is uniformly \(L\)-Lipschitz on the disturbance space.
\(P\) and \(\widetilde P\) have finite first moments.
Both optimal values are finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|v(P)-v(\widetilde P)|\le L W_1(P,\widetilde P)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Wasserstein-Lipschitz estimate is plausible, but the optimization problems defining the two optimal values are only implicit and no scenario-reduction source is cited.

children.title: Parallel Work Complexity
children.top_down_role: Aggregate computational effort across all workers.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Work Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work–span accounting for a parallel decomposition computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Represent a decomposition computation by a directed acyclic task graph. Let \(W\) be the sum of all task costs and \(D\) the maximum cost of any dependency path. On \(p\ge1\) identical processors, every valid schedule has running time
\[
T_p\ge\max\{W/p,D\}.
\]
A greedy work-conserving schedule satisfies \(T_p\le W/p+D\) up to the adopted task-cost convention. Hence parallel work complexity is \(W\), while processor-time is bounded by \(pT_p\le W+pD\); useful scaling requires both sufficient available parallelism \(W/D\) and controlled scheduling overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total task work and critical-path depth bound parallel runtime; adding processors helps only while available parallelism and overhead permit it.
assumptions_latex: Tasks form a finite directed acyclic graph.
Processors are identical and execute ready tasks greedily.
Task costs include the chosen local computation overhead.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{W/p,D\}\le T_p\le W/p+D\).

children.title: Critical-Path Depth
children.top_down_role: Sequential dependency depth limiting completion time.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Path Depth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted dependency depth of a parallel decomposition task graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed acyclic task graph, with task cost \(w_v\ge0\) for each \(v\in V\). Its critical-path depth is
\[
D(G)=\max_{P}\sum_{v\in P}w_v,
\]
where the maximum ranges over all directed paths \(P\) in \(G\). Because precedence constraints force the tasks on every directed path to execute sequentially, any execution on any number of processors has elapsed time \(T_p\ge D(G)\). For unit-cost tasks, \(D(G)\) equals the maximum number of vertices on a directed path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Critical-path depth is the greatest accumulated task cost along any dependency path and is an unavoidable lower bound on parallel runtime.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
Each task has cost \(w_v\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_p\ge D(G)=\max_P\sum_{v\in P}w_v\).

children.title: Parallel Speedup
children.top_down_role: Runtime improvement relative to a designated sequential baseline.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Speedup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amdahl-model speedup and its serial-fraction ceiling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T_1>0\) be serial runtime and suppose a fraction \(s\in[0,1]\) is inherently serial while the remaining fraction parallelizes perfectly over \(p\ge1\) processors. Then
\[
T_p=T_1\left(s+\frac{1-s}{p}\right),
\qquad
S_p=\frac{T_1}{T_p}=\frac{1}{s+(1-s)/p}.
\]
If \(s>0\), then \(S_p\le1/s\) and \(\lim_{p\to\infty}S_p=1/s\). Thus any nonzero serial coordination fraction imposes a finite ceiling on the parallel speedup of the decomposition computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Amdahl's model, speedup is the reciprocal of serial fraction plus parallel fraction divided by processors, and cannot exceed the inverse serial fraction.
assumptions_latex: A fraction \(s\) of serial runtime cannot be parallelized.
The remaining fraction has perfect load balance and no added overhead.

notation.meaning: parallel speedup relative to one processor

children.title: Coordination-Limited Scaling
children.top_down_role: Speedup limits caused by master work, synchronization, or communication.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordination-Limited Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Speedup ceiling induced by processor-dependent coordination time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a computation have perfectly divisible work \(W>0\) and unavoidable coordination time \(C(p)\ge0\) on \(p\ge1\) processors. If
\[
T_p\ge \frac{W}{p}+C(p),
\]
then its speedup relative to work time \(W\) satisfies
\[
S_p=\frac{W}{T_p}\le\frac{W}{W/p+C(p)}.
\]
In particular, if \(C(p)\ge c>0\), then \(S_p\le W/c\). If \(C(p)\to\infty\) as \(p\to\infty\), then the upper bound \(W/(W/p+C(p))\) tends to zero. Hence processor growth alone cannot ensure useful scaling when synchronization, aggregation, or master coordination dominates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel speedup is bounded by divisible work plus coordination time; persistent coordination imposes a finite ceiling, and diverging coordination drives the stated upper bound to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(W>0\) is perfectly divisible computational work.
\(p\in\mathbb N\) and \(p\ge1\).
\(C(p)\ge0\) is unavoidable coordination time.

children.title: Communication-Volume Complexity
children.top_down_role: Scaling in transferred data across decomposed workers.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Volume Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total transmitted payload in a distributed decomposition execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For messages \(m=1,
\ldots,M\) transmitted during an execution, with payload size \(b_m\ge0\) measured in words or bytes, the communication volume is
\[
V=\sum_{m=1}^{M}b_m.
\]
If message \(m\) traverses \(h_m\) network links, the link-volume measure is \(V_{\rm link}=\sum_m h_mb_m\). Under an \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) communication model with \(R\) nonoverlapped communication rounds, elapsed communication time is bounded below by \(\alpha R+\beta V_\ast\), where \(V_\ast\) is the maximum payload volume carried by any processor or bottleneck link.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication volume sums transmitted payloads; network time also depends on rounds, latency, and the most heavily loaded processor or link.
assumptions_latex: Payload sizes use a fixed word or byte convention.
Communication rounds do not overlap in the stated time model.
\(\alpha,\beta\ge0\) are latency and inverse-bandwidth parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V=\sum_m b_m\) and \(T_{\rm comm}\ge\alpha R+\beta V_\ast\).

children.title: Communication-Round Complexity
children.top_down_role: Scaling in distinct coordination exchanges.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Round Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential communication phases required by a distributed decomposition algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a distributed decomposition algorithm \(A\). Partition its communication into rounds so that messages sent in round \(r\) may depend only on local state and messages received before round \(r\). Let \(R_A(\varepsilon)\) be the number of rounds in the prescribed execution that first outputs a valid \(\varepsilon\)-certificate, and let \(K_A(\varepsilon)\) be its number of completed decomposition iterations. If every completed iteration necessarily contains exactly \(q\in\mathbb N_0\) causally sequential, nonoverlappable communication phases and no additional communication rounds occur, then
\[
R_A(\varepsilon)=qK_A(\varepsilon).
\]
Consequently, if each round incurs unavoidable latency \(\alpha\ge0\), then latency contributes at least \(\alpha qK_A(\varepsilon)\) to elapsed time, independently of payload size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed algorithm, q mandatory sequential communication phases per iteration and no additional rounds yield q times the iteration count, with a corresponding latency cost.
assumptions_latex: Rounds permit parallel messages but impose causal separation from later rounds.
Each completed iteration has exactly \(q\in\mathbb N_0\) mandatory sequential communication phases.
No additional communication rounds occur outside those phases.
The prescribed execution outputs a valid \(\varepsilon\)-certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_A(\varepsilon)=qK_A(\varepsilon)\) and \(T_{\rm latency}\ge\alpha R_A(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: communication rounds used by algorithm A to reach tolerance epsilon
iterations used by algorithm A to reach tolerance epsilon
mandatory sequential communication phases per iteration

children.title: Synchronization Complexity
children.top_down_role: Cost of barriers, waiting, or globally aligned progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts global barriers and the mean worker waiting caused by imbalance in synchronous decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a decomposition algorithm executed for \(K\) coordination epochs on \(p\) workers. Let \(b_k\) be the number of global barriers in epoch \(k\), and, for \(\ell\in\{1,\ldots,b_k\}\), let \(t_{ik\ell}\) be worker \(i\)'s arrival time at barrier \(\ell\), measured from a common origin for that barrier. Define
\[N_{\mathrm{sync}}(K)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}b_k\]
and
\[W_{\mathrm{sync}}(K)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{b_k}\left(\max_{1\le i\le p}t_{ik\ell}-\frac1p\sum_{i=1}^{p}t_{ik\ell}\right).\]
Thus \(N_{\mathrm{sync}}(K)\) counts synchronization events, while \(W_{\mathrm{sync}}(K)\) accumulates the mean per-worker waiting time at those barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization complexity comprises the number of global barriers and the accumulated mean delay between worker arrival times and the slowest arrival at each barrier.
assumptions_latex: \(K,p\in\mathbb N\) with \(K,p\ge1\).
\(b_k\in\mathbb N_0\) and \(t_{ik\ell}\ge0\) for every defined worker, epoch, and barrier index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{sync}}(K)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}b_k\) and \(W_{\mathrm{sync}}(K)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{b_k}(\max_i t_{ik\ell}-p^{-1}\sum_i t_{ik\ell})\).

notation.meaning: number of global barriers in coordination epoch k
arrival time of worker i at barrier ell of epoch k
accumulated mean per-worker barrier waiting time

children.title: Latency-Dominated Scaling
children.top_down_role: Regimes where coordination latency dominates local computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Latency-Dominated Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the regime where coordination startup latency controls distributed runtime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p\) workers, write the runtime model as
\[T_p=F_p+\beta V_p+\alpha R_p,\]
where \(F_p\) is local computation time, \(V_p\) is communicated volume, \(\beta\) is inverse bandwidth, \(R_p\) is the number of communication rounds, and \(\alpha\) is per-round latency. A scaling sequence is latency dominated when
\[\frac{F_p+\beta V_p}{\alpha R_p}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }p\to\infty.\]
In that regime, \(T_p/(\alpha R_p)\to1\); consequently, reducing local work or message volume alone cannot improve the leading-order runtime unless it also reduces rounds or latency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling is latency dominated when round-startup time asymptotically exceeds both local computation and bandwidth-dependent transfer time.
assumptions_latex: \(F_p,V_p,R_p\ge0\), \(\alpha>0\), and \(\beta\ge0\).
\(R_p>0\) along the scaling sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((F_p+\beta V_p)/(\alpha R_p)\to0\implies T_p/(\alpha R_p)\to1\).

children.title: Synchronous Master–Worker Coordination
children.top_down_role: Master updates formed from globally aligned worker returns.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronous Master–Worker Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier-synchronous coordination for separable subproblem information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be the master-state space, let \(Y_i\) be worker \(i\)'s response space for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\), and let \(G_i:X\to Y_i\), \(A:X\times Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_p\to X\), and \(S:X\times Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_p\to\{0,1\}\). Given \(x^0\in X\), epoch \(k\) proceeds by broadcasting \(x^k\), computing \(y_i^k=G_i(x^k)\) at every worker, and waiting until all \(p\) responses arrive. The master then sets
\[x^{k+1}=A(x^k,y_1^k,\ldots,y_p^k).\]
If \(S(x^{k+1},y_1^k,\ldots,y_p^k)=1\), it outputs \(x^{k+1}\); otherwise it begins epoch \(k+1\). No response computed from another epoch enters the update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each epoch broadcasts one master state, waits for every worker response, aggregates only responses computed from that state, and then tests termination.
assumptions_latex: \(p\in\mathbb N\) with \(p\ge1\), and \(x^0\in X\).
The maps \(G_i:X\to Y_i\), \(A:X\times Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_p\to X\), and \(S:X\times Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_p\to\{0,1\}\) are defined on every generated argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}=A(x^k,G_1(x^k),\ldots,G_p(x^k))\) after an all-worker barrier.

children.title: Asynchronous Master–Worker Coordination
children.top_down_role: Master updates formed from independently timed worker returns.

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous Master–Worker Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-driven master updates without an all-worker barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be the master-state space, let \(Y_i\) be the response space of worker \(i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\), let \(G_i:X\to Y_i\), let \(A_i:X\times Y_i\to X\), and let \(S:X\times\mathbb N_0\to\{0,1\}\) be a stopping predicate. Initialize \(x^0\in X\), set the update counter to \(k=0\), and send one task carrying \(x^0\) to each worker. Whenever worker \(i_k\) returns \(y^k=G_{i_k}(x^{s_k})\), where \(s_k\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\) is the version used by that worker, the master immediately sets
\[x^{k+1}=A_{i_k}(x^k,y^k),\]
increments \(k\), and sends a new task carrying the current state to the available worker. Other workers continue without a barrier. If \(S(x^k,k)=1\), the master outputs \(x^k\); otherwise it processes the next arriving response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The master updates on each arriving worker response, records the state version used to compute it, and dispatches new work without waiting for all workers.
assumptions_latex: \(p\in\mathbb N\) with \(p\ge1\), and \(x^0\in X\).
\(s_k\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\) for every accepted response.
The maps \(G_i:X\to Y_i\), \(A_i:X\times Y_i\to X\), and \(S:X\times\mathbb N_0\to\{0,1\}\) are defined on every generated argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}=A_{i_k}(x^k,G_{i_k}(x^{s_k}))\) without an all-worker barrier.

notation.meaning: master-state version used for update k's arriving response
worker whose response triggers update k

children.title: Partially Synchronous Coordination
children.top_down_role: Coordination using bounded waiting, quotas, or partial return sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Partially Synchronous Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quorum coordination with a finite accepted-staleness bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a quorum size \(q\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and staleness bound \(\tau\in\mathbb N_0\). At epoch \(k\), the master broadcasts \(x^k\) and accepts responses \(y_i=G_i(x^{s_i})\) only when \(k-\tau\le s_i\le k\). Once responses from a set \(Q_k\) of \(q\) distinct workers have arrived, it updates
\[x^{k+1}=A(x^k,(y_i)_{i\in Q_k}),\]
without waiting for the remaining workers. Responses older than \(k-	au\) are discarded or recomputed. The algorithm outputs the first \(x^k\) satisfying its prescribed stopping test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The master waits for a quorum rather than every worker, while rejecting responses older than a fixed version bound.
assumptions_latex: \(p\in\mathbb N\), \(1\le q\le p\), and \(\tau\in\mathbb N_0\).
A qualifying quorum eventually arrives at every nonterminal epoch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|Q_k|=q\) and \(0\le k-s_i\le\tau\) for every \(i\in Q_k\).

notation.meaning: number of distinct responses required for an update

children.title: Staleness-Control Boundary
children.top_down_role: Operational limits imposed by outdated worker contributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Staleness-Control Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that unrestricted reuse of obsolete versions lies outside the standard uniformly bounded-staleness regime and can defeat convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an accepted response computed from version \(s_k\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\), define its staleness by \(d_k=k-s_k\). A common bounded-staleness regime assumes that some finite \(\tau\in\mathbb N_0\) satisfies \(d_k\le\tau\) for every accepted update, typically together with a suitable worker-activation condition. Without any control on obsolete reads, convergence can fail even for a contraction. Let \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(T(x)=x/2\), set \(x^0=1\), and use \(s_k=0\) in every update. Then
\[x^{k+1}=T(x^{s_k})=\tfrac12\quad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb N_0,\]
although the unique fixed point of \(T\) is \(0\). Thus unrestricted reuse of obsolete states does not inherit the usual synchronous contraction conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly bounded delay is a common staleness-control regime; without any control on obsolete reads, an asynchronous iteration can fail to converge even when its map is a contraction.
assumptions_latex: \(s_k\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\) and \(d_k=k-s_k\).
The asynchronous update is \(x^{k+1}=T(x^{s_k})\).
In the counterexample, \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(T(x)=x/2\), \(x^0=1\), and \(s_k=0\) for every \(k\in\mathbb N_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_k(k-s_k)=\infty\) can permit \(x^k\not\to x^\star\) even when \(T\) is contractive.

notation.meaning: fixed-point map used by the asynchronous iteration

children.title: Block Bundling
children.top_down_role: Grouping decision blocks for assignment or joint local solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Bundling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bundles separable optimization blocks into larger coordinated units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) index separable blocks with variables \(x_j\in X_j\), local objectives \(f_j\), and coupling through \(\sum_{j\in J}A_jx_j=b\). A block bundling is a partition \(\mathcal B=\{B_1,\ldots,B_r\}\) of \(J\). For each bundle \(B\in\mathcal B\), define
\[x_B=(x_j)_{j\in B},\qquad F_B(x_B)=\sum_{j\in B}f_j(x_j),\qquad A_Bx_B=\sum_{j\in B}A_jx_j.\]
The bundled formulation replaces individual block units by the \(r\) aggregate units while preserving the original objective and coupling equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block bundling partitions separable blocks and represents each group by its product variable, summed objective, and aggregated coupling contribution.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and \(\mathcal B\) is a partition of \(J\).
Each displayed sum and product-space variable is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{B\in\mathcal B}F_B(x_B)=\sum_{j\in J}f_j(x_j)\) and \(\sum_{B\in\mathcal B}A_Bx_B=\sum_{j\in J}A_jx_j\).

notation.meaning: aggregate coupling contribution of bundle B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partition construction is internally correct and fits the leaf, but no citation supports the use of this construction as block bundling in decomposition orchestration.

children.title: Scenario Bundling
children.top_down_role: Grouping uncertainty scenarios into shared computational units.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Bundling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregates stochastic-program scenarios within partition cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\) be a finite scenario set with probabilities \(p_\omega>0\), \(\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p_\omega=1\), and recourse values \(Q_\omega(x)\). A scenario bundling is a partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(\Omega\). For each bundle \(B\in\mathcal P\), set
\[p_B=\sum_{\omega\in B}p_\omega,\qquad Q_B(x)=p_B^{-1}\sum_{\omega\in B}p_\omega Q_\omega(x).\]
Then the expected recourse has the exact bundled representation
\[\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p_\omega Q_\omega(x)=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}p_BQ_B(x).\]
Bundling changes the coordination units, not the represented expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario bundling partitions scenarios and replaces each group by its probability mass and conditional weighted recourse, preserving expected recourse exactly.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) is finite and every \(p_\omega>0\).
\(Q_\omega(x)\) is finite for the point under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p_\omega Q_\omega(x)=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}p_BQ_B(x)\).

notation.meaning: probability mass of scenario bundle B
conditional weighted recourse of bundle B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expectation identity is correct, but no cited stochastic-decomposition source establishes this exact partition-and-conditional-average construction as scenario bundling in the target sense.

children.title: Cut Bundling
children.top_down_role: Grouping generated inequalities for transfer or master insertion.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Bundling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Groups valid master inequalities without altering their intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a relaxation and let \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), indexed by a finite set \(I\), be valid for the target feasible set. A cut bundling is a partition \(\mathcal C\) of \(I\) together with storage or transmission of each group \(C\in\mathcal C\) as one coordination unit. If every member cut remains enforced, the bundled master region is
\[P_{\mathcal C}=P\cap\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal C}\bigcap_{i\in C}\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\}=P\cap\bigcap_{i\in I}\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\}.\]
Hence grouping alone changes orchestration but not the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut bundling partitions valid inequalities into coordination units; retaining every member inequality leaves the master relaxation unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite and \(\mathcal C\) partitions \(I\).
Every member cut is retained and enforced exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathcal C}=P\cap\bigcap_{i\in I}\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\}\).

notation.meaning: partition of the cut index set
master region under bundled cut organization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set identity is correct when all inequalities remain individually enforced, but no source supports this storage or transmission organization as cut bundling in decomposition practice.

children.title: Mixed-Granularity Bundling
children.top_down_role: Coordinated bundling choices across multiple decomposed object types.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Granularity Bundling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allows simultaneously unequal and dynamically refined decomposition bundles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\) be a finite set of atomic decomposition units. A mixed-granularity bundling at epoch \(k\) is a partition \(\mathcal B_k\) of \(J\) whose cells may have unequal cardinalities and may change between epochs. A transition from \(\mathcal B_k\) to \(\mathcal B_{k+1}\) is admissible when every new cell is a union of atoms and the new cells remain disjoint with union \(J\). For additive data \(g_j\), each bundle carries
\[g_B=\sum_{j\in B}g_j,\qquad B\in\mathcal B_k.\]
Consequently, \(\sum_{B\in\mathcal B_k}g_B=\sum_{j\in J}g_j\) at every epoch, despite heterogeneous granularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed-granularity bundling uses unequal, possibly changing groups of atomic units while preserving a partition and additive aggregate data.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
Each \(\mathcal B_k\) is a partition of \(J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{B\in\mathcal B_k}\sum_{j\in B}g_j=\sum_{j\in J}g_j\) for every epoch \(k\).

notation.meaning: additive data aggregated over bundle B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partition identity is valid, but no source establishes that unequal, epoch-varying partitions are the intended mathematical meaning of mixed-granularity bundling in this decomposition taxonomy.

children.title: Dynamic Load Balancing
children.top_down_role: Adaptive redistribution of decomposed computational work.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Load Balancing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online assignment of ready decomposition tasks to heterogeneous workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\) be a queue of ready tasks, let worker \(i\) have estimated service rate \(v_i>0\), and let \(L_i\) be its assigned unfinished work, initialized to zero. Whenever a worker becomes available or a task becomes ready, assign a task \(j\in Q\) with estimated work \(w_j>0\) to a worker minimizing
\[\frac{L_i+w_j}{v_i}.\]
Remove \(j\) from \(Q\), increase \(L_i\) by \(w_j\), and decrease \(L_i\) as work completes. Update estimates from observed service times. Stop when \(Q\) is empty and all \(L_i=0\); output the collected decomposition responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ready tasks are assigned online to the worker with the smallest predicted normalized completion load, using service-time observations to update estimates.
assumptions_latex: Each assigned task eventually completes or is explicitly reassigned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(j\) is assigned to an element of \(\operatorname*{argmin}_i (L_i+w_j)/v_i\).

notation.meaning: estimated service rate of worker i
unfinished work assigned to worker i

children.title: Straggler Detection
children.top_down_role: Identification of persistently slow workers or subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Straggler Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust elapsed-time rule for flagging unusually slow active workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a common checkpoint, let \(e_i\ge0\) be the elapsed processing time of active worker \(i\), and let \(H\) contain at least three recently completed comparable task times. Define the robust baseline
\[m=\operatorname{median}(H),\qquad d=\operatorname{median}\{|h-m|:h\in H\}.\]
For a chosen multiplier \(c>0\) and minimum timeout \(t_{\min}>0\), worker \(i\) is declared a straggler precisely when
\[e_i>\theta,\qquad \theta=\max\{t_{\min},m+cd\}.\]
The comparison class, multiplier, and timeout must be fixed before the declaration; the predicate detects delay but does not itself establish worker failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A worker is flagged when its elapsed time exceeds a fixed minimum and a robust median-plus-deviation threshold computed from comparable completed tasks.
assumptions_latex: \(|H|\ge3\) and every \(h\in H\) is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(i\) is flagged if and only if \(e_i>\max\{t_{\min},m+cd\}\).

notation.meaning: reference sample of comparable task times
sample median and median absolute deviation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The median-plus-MAD predicate is mathematically well defined, but it is only one possible detector and has no citation establishing it as the intended straggler-detection condition for this leaf.

children.title: Straggler Mitigation
children.top_down_role: Operational responses such as reassignment, replication, or partial acceptance.

knowledge_statements.title: Straggler Mitigation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deadline-and-reassignment rule for independent decomposition subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given tasks \(J\), workers \(W\), deadline \(\tau>0\), and replication limit \(r\ge 1\), assign each \(j\in J\) to one worker. If task \(j\) has not returned by age \(\tau\), dispatch it to an additional available worker while fewer than \(r\) copies are active. Accept the first valid result \(z_j\), cancel its remaining copies, and discard every later result carrying the same task-version identifier. Terminate when one valid result has been accepted for every task required by the current decomposition iteration; output \((z_j)_{j\in J}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicate overdue independent tasks, accept the first version-valid result, cancel duplicates, and finish after every required task has one accepted result.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and its tasks are independently executable for a fixed iteration state.
Every returned result carries an immutable task-version identifier.
Cancellation or duplicate suppression is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{At most one version-valid result per task is incorporated.}\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: first-result acceptance with version checks is a standard speculative-execution rule

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the Straggler Mitigation leaf and is internally coherent, but the precise deadline, bounded-replication, first-result, cancellation, and version-suppression policy has no cited source.

children.title: Heterogeneous-Worker Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous-Worker Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic capacity model for heterogeneous decomposition workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A worker system \(W\) is heterogeneous for a task family \(J\) if each worker \(w\in W\) has an admissibility set \(A_w\subseteq J\), service-rate function \(s_w:J	o[0,\infty)\), and availability fraction \(a_w\in[0,1]\), and there exist \(u,v\in W\) and \(j\in A_u\cap A_v\) such that \(a_u s_u(j)
e a_v s_v(j)\), or \(A_u
e A_v\). A feasible assignment \(x_{wj}\in\{0,1\}\) satisfies \(x_{wj}=0\) for \(j
otin A_w\) and \(\sum_{w\in W}x_{wj}=1\) for every \(j\in J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers are heterogeneous when effective service rates or task eligibility differ; a feasible assignment sends each task to exactly one eligible worker.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) and \(J\) are finite.
Service rates and availability fractions are fixed during the scheduling epoch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W\text{ is heterogeneous exactly under the displayed rate-or-eligibility predicate.}\)

children.title: Warm-Start State
children.top_down_role: Reusable solution information transferred between related solves.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reusable initialization state for a parameterized decomposition subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a parameterized solver map \(\mathcal S(d,q)\), where \(d\) is the current problem data and \(q\) is initialization data, a warm-start state is a tuple \(q=(x,
u,B,H,\sigma)\) retained from an earlier solve. Its components may contain a primal point \(x\), dual multipliers \(\nu\), a basis identifier \(B\), curvature information \(H\), and solver metadata \(\sigma\). The state is admissible for new data \(d'\) only if every retained component has the dimensions, indexing, and solver semantics required by \(\mathcal S(d',\cdot)\); otherwise that component must be discarded or transformed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A warm start stores compatible primal, dual, basis, curvature, and solver metadata from an earlier solve for initializing a related problem.
assumptions_latex: The solver exposes an initialization-state interface.
Compatibility can be checked before the new solve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\text{ may initialize }\mathcal S(d',q)\text{ only after compatibility validation.}\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: warm starts conventionally retain compatible solver iterates and auxiliary state
source required for the decomposition-specific state tuple

children.title: Basis Reuse
children.top_down_role: Persistence of linear-programming basis information across master or subproblem changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validated reuse of a simplex basis after subproblem modification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a linear program \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and a stored basis index set \(B\) with \(|B|=m\), first verify that the columns indexed by \(B\) still exist and that \(A_B\) is nonsingular. Compute \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\) and the reduced costs \(\bar c_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\). If \(x_B\ge0\), initialize primal simplex from \(B\); if \(\bar c_N\ge0\), initialize dual simplex from \(B\); otherwise use \(B\) only through a solver-supported repair procedure. If validation fails, discard \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reuse a stored LP basis only after structural and nonsingularity checks, selecting primal, dual, or repaired initialization according to feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has row rank \(m\).
The minimization problem is in equality-form standard form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is reused only when it remains a nonsingular basis with a supported initialization status.}\)

notation.meaning: basic and nonbasic column index sets

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: primal and dual simplex starts are characterized by basic and reduced-cost feasibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and standard-form calculations are mathematically plausible and fit Basis Reuse, but no authoritative simplex warm-start source is cited for the validation and repair policy.

children.title: Worker-Local State
children.top_down_role: Cached solver, model, or generated-object state retained by workers.

knowledge_statements.title: Worker-Local State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Versioned solver state owned by one decomposition worker.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For workers \(W\), a worker-local state is a family \((q_w)_{w\in W}\) with \(q_w=(v_w,D_w,S_w)\), where \(v_w\) is the master-state version, \(D_w\) identifies the subproblem data assigned to worker \(w\), and \(S_w\) contains reusable solver information. Worker \(w\) may update only \(q_w\). A result computed from \(q_w\) is admissible to the coordinator only when its reported version equals the coordinator's required version and \(D_w\) identifies the requested task; local solver information need not be globally synchronized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each worker privately owns versioned task and solver state; the coordinator accepts its result only when task identity and version match.
assumptions_latex: Each worker has a unique identifier in \(W\).
Messages carry task and master-state versions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Acceptance requires matching task identity and master-state version.}\)

notation.meaning: master-state version used by worker w

children.title: State-Invalidation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Model changes that make retained state unreliable or unusable.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Invalidation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predicate determining when retained solver state cannot be reused directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\) be retained state created for data \(d\), and let \(d'\) be new data. Define \(\operatorname{valid}(q;d,d')\) to hold precisely when all referenced variables and constraints preserve their identifiers and dimensions, every stored algebraic object remains defined for \(d'\), and every solver-specific invariant attached to \(q\) remains satisfied. The state-invalidation boundary is the set \(\mathcal I_q=\{d':\neg\operatorname{valid}(q;d,d')\}\). For \(d'\in\mathcal I_q\), direct reuse is forbidden; the state must be projected, repaired by a validated transformation, or discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: New data cross the invalidation boundary when retained state loses structural, algebraic, or solver-semantic compatibility; direct reuse is then forbidden.
assumptions_latex: The retained state records its referenced identifiers, dimensions, and invariants.
A deterministic compatibility test is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d'\in\mathcal I_q\Longrightarrow q\text{ is not directly reusable for }d'.\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reusable computational state requires structural and semantic compatibility
source required for a canonical decomposition-specific invalidation predicate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf and is internally consistent, but the comprehensive validity predicate and mandatory project-repair-discard response are uncited, bespoke rules.

children.title: Cut-Pool Management
children.top_down_role: Retention, activation, aging, and removal of generated cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Pool Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity-preserving selection and deletion policy for decomposition cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a pool \(P_k\) of globally valid inequalities \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\ge b_i\), each with age \(g_i\) and last violation \(v_i(x_k)=\max\{0,b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x_k\}\). At iteration \(k\), insert newly certified cuts, merge positive scalar duplicates, and activate every cut with \(v_i(x_k)>\varepsilon\), together with at most \(M\) inactive cuts ranked by violation or recent activity. Increment \(g_i\) for inactive cuts and reset it for active cuts. A cut may be deleted only if its validity is not needed for correctness and \(g_i>G\). Output the selected active pool.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insert certified cuts, merge duplicates, prioritize violated or recently active cuts, and delete only old cuts whose retention is unnecessary for correctness.
assumptions_latex: Every inserted inequality is globally valid for the feasible set.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\), \(M\in\mathbb N\), and \(G\in\mathbb N\) are fixed.
The underlying method identifies cuts that must be retained for correctness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Every active cut is valid, and protected cuts are never deleted.}\)

notation.meaning: violation of cut i at the current point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cut pools commonly use validity, violation, duplication, and age criteria
source required for the precise retention policy and its correctness boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Cut-Pool Management, but its exact activation cap, duplicate merging, aging, protection, and deletion policy lacks a supporting source and depends on an unspecified correctness-retention classification.

children.title: Column-Pool Management
children.top_down_role: Retention, activation, aging, and removal of generated columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Column-Pool Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-cost-based activation policy for generated master columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimization restricted master problem, maintain a pool \(P_k\) of feasible columns \(p
e0\) with cost \(c_p\). Given current dual vector \(y_k\), compute reduced cost \(\bar c_p=c_p-y_k^{\mathsf T}p\). Insert newly priced columns, merge identical columns while retaining the least cost, and activate all columns with \(\bar c_p< -\varepsilon\), subject to a cap \(M\) by increasing reduced cost. A basic column is protected from deletion. An inactive nonbasic column may be deleted after \(G\) consecutive iterations without qualifying for activation. Output the active restricted-master column set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Manage feasible generated columns by reduced cost, duplicate suppression, capacity limits, and protection of basic columns.
assumptions_latex: The restricted master is a minimization linear program.
Every pooled column satisfies the master column-domain constraints.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\), \(M\in\mathbb N\), and \(G\in\mathbb N\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Every activated column is feasible, and every sufficiently improving pooled column is eligible for activation.}\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reduced cost is the standard activation criterion in linear-programming column generation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Column-Pool Management and uses the standard reduced-cost sign for minimization, but the precise capped activation, duplicate handling, aging, and deletion rules are unsupported.

children.title: Scenario-Pool Management
children.top_down_role: Retention, prioritization, and reuse of sampled or discovered scenarios.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Pool Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection policy for finite scenario subproblems under a certified coverage rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\) be a finite scenario set with weights \(p_\omega>0\), and maintain active set \(A_k\subseteq\Omega\) and last-known residuals \(r_\omega^k\ge0\). At iteration \(k\), activate every scenario with \(r_\omega^k>\varepsilon\), add sampled inactive scenarios according to a distribution assigning positive probability to each member of \(\Omega\), and solve the resulting subproblems. Update their residuals and ages. A scenario may be deactivated after \(G\) consecutive solves with residual at most \(\varepsilon\), but termination is permitted only after every scenario has been evaluated at the candidate solution or an equivalent valid global certificate is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prioritize scenarios with large residuals, sample all others with positive probability, and require complete evaluation or a global certificate before termination.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) is finite and \(p_\omega>0\) for every \(\omega\in\Omega\).
Residuals are nonnegative and computable by solving the selected scenario subproblem.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(G\in\mathbb N\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Pool reduction cannot itself certify termination without complete coverage or an equivalent certificate.}\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: residual prioritization must be separated from a valid termination-coverage condition
source required for the stated finite-scenario pool policy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Scenario-Pool Management, but the residual-based activation, randomized sampling, deactivation threshold, and termination-coverage rule form a specific uncited policy whose validity depends on the underlying decomposition method.

children.title: Cross-Pool Coordination
children.top_down_role: Interactions among multiple generated-object repositories.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Pool Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Version-consistent coordination of cut, column, and scenario pools.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At major iteration \(k\), freeze a master version \(v_k\) and select scenario set \(S_k\), column set \(C_k\), and cut set \(K_k\). Solve the restricted master on \((C_k,K_k)\), price columns using its dual solution, and evaluate selected scenarios using its primal solution. Tag every generated object with \(v_k\). Before insertion, validate each cut against the current variable space, each column against the current constraint space, and each scenario result against the current candidate. If a structural change makes a tagged object undefined, invalidate or transform it before reuse. Advance to \(v_{k+1}\) only after all accepted updates are committed atomically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate scenario, column, and cut pools through one master version, validating generated objects before an atomic version advance.
assumptions_latex: Every generated object records its originating master version.
Structural compatibility and mathematical validity are separately testable.
Pool updates can be committed atomically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{No object is incorporated into a master version for which it is undefined or unvalidated.}\)

notation.meaning: master version at major iteration k
selected scenario, column, and cut sets

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: mixed decomposition artifacts require version and space compatibility
source required for a canonical cross-pool transaction rule

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Cross-Pool Coordination, but the unified versioning, compatibility validation, transformation, and atomic-commit protocol is a bespoke orchestration rule without supporting evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Generation-Preferred Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition favoring delayed constraint generation over full enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_t(x)\le0\ \forall t\in T\}\), where the full constraint family \(T\) is too large to enumerate. A cut-generation regime is applicable when, for every trial point \(x\in X\), an oracle either certifies \(g_t(x)\le0\) for all \(t\in T\) or returns an index \(t_x\) with \(g_{t_x}(x)>0\), and the returned inequality is valid for the original feasible set. It is preferred to explicit enumeration when the restricted problems remain tractable and oracle-plus-reoptimization cost is smaller than constructing and solving the full formulation under the chosen resource metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prefer cut generation when constraints are numerous, violated valid inequalities can be separated, restricted problems remain tractable, and delayed enforcement costs less than enumeration.
assumptions_latex: Every oracle-generated inequality is valid for the original feasible set.
Restricted problems over finite subsets of \(T\) can be solved to the required accuracy.
A common time or memory metric compares decomposition with full enumeration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The model lies in the cut-generation-preferred regime under the displayed oracle and cost conditions.}\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: separation access and economical restricted reoptimization characterize delayed constraint generation
source required for the comparative preference criterion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the regime-selection leaf and correctly distinguishes applicability from comparative preference, but the claimed preference criterion requires a source defining or supporting the oracle and resource-cost comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Column-Generation-Preferred Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition favoring delayed variable generation over full enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a linear master problem whose feasible variables are indexed by a set \(P\) too large to enumerate. For each restricted set \(P_k\subset P\), let \(y_k\) be an optimal dual solution. A column-generation regime is applicable when a pricing oracle either returns \(p\in P\) with reduced cost \(\bar c_p(y_k)<-\varepsilon\) or certifies \(\bar c_p(y_k)\ge-\varepsilon\) for all \(p\in P\). It is preferred to explicit enumeration when restricted masters remain tractable and the cumulative pricing-plus-reoptimization cost is smaller than generating and solving the full master under the selected time or memory metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prefer column generation when variables are numerous, pricing can find or exclude improving columns, restricted masters are tractable, and delayed generation is cheaper.
assumptions_latex: The master is a minimization linear program with well-defined reduced costs.
The pricing oracle is exact to tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
A common time or memory metric compares decomposition with full enumeration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The model lies in the column-generation-preferred regime under the displayed pricing and cost conditions.}\)

notation.meaning: reduced cost of column p at dual solution y_k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pricing access and economical restricted-master solution characterize delayed variable generation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf and states a coherent minimization pricing test, but no authoritative column-generation source supports the exact tolerance certificate and comparative preference criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Consensus-Preferred Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-based selection condition for finite-scenario convex programs admitting scenario copies and consensus constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be finite and consider \(\min_{x\in X}\sum_{s\in S}p_s f_s(x)\), equivalently \(\min_{z,\{x_s\}}\sum_{s\in S}p_s f_s(x_s)\) subject to \(x_s=z\in X\). Let \(C_{\mathrm{SC}}(\varepsilon)\) denote the estimated parallel work plus communication needed by a convergent consensus method to produce an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate solution, and let \(C_m(\varepsilon)\) denote the corresponding cost for each eligible alternative \(m\). The scenario-consensus-preferred regime is the set of instances for which scenario subproblems are independently solvable and \[C_{\mathrm{SC}}(\varepsilon)\leq \min_m C_m(\varepsilon).\] Ineligible alternatives are assigned infinite cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario consensus is preferred when scenarios separate after copying shared variables and its estimated parallel computation and communication cost is no greater than every eligible alternative.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite, \(p_s>0\), and \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\).
\(X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and every \(f_s\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The compared costs use the same accuracy criterion \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{SC}}(\varepsilon)\leq\min_m C_m(\varepsilon)\) characterizes the scenario-consensus-preferred region among eligible methods.

notation.meaning: scenario-local decision and shared consensus decision
estimated total cost of method m at accuracy epsilon

knowledge_statements.title: Monolithic Extensive-Form-Preferred Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-based selection condition for solving a finite block-structured formulation without decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the extensive form be \(\min\{F(y):y\in Y,\ Ay=b\}\), where \(y\) contains all block variables and \(Ay=b\) contains their linking constraints. Let \(C_{\mathrm{EF}}(\varepsilon)\) be the estimated memory and arithmetic cost of solving this formulation directly to accuracy \(\varepsilon\); let \(C_d(\varepsilon)\) include master iterations, subproblem work, and communication for each eligible decomposition \(d\). The monolithic extensive-form-preferred regime consists of instances fitting available memory and satisfying \[C_{\mathrm{EF}}(\varepsilon)\leq\min_d C_d(\varepsilon).\] Thus decomposition overhead is not justified under the common cost and accuracy conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extensive form is preferred when it fits memory and its direct-solve cost does not exceed the full iteration, subproblem, and communication cost of any decomposition.
assumptions_latex: The extensive form is finite-dimensional and represents the original optimization problem exactly.
All compared methods use the same accuracy criterion \(\varepsilon\).
Cost estimates include memory feasibility and all method-specific overhead.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Memory feasibility together with \(C_{\mathrm{EF}}(\varepsilon)\leq\min_d C_d(\varepsilon)\) defines the monolithic-preferred region.

children.title: Cut–Column Hybrid Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Cut–Column Hybrid Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural and cost conditions for combining constraint generation with variable generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:x\in\operatorname{conv}(V),\ a_i^Tx\geq b_i\ (i\in I)\}\), where both \(V\) and \(I\) may be too large to enumerate. A cut–column method maintains finite sets \(V_k\subset V\) and \(I_k\subset I\), solves the restricted master over \(\operatorname{conv}(V_k)\), and invokes separation and pricing oracles to enlarge \(I_k\) and \(V_k\). This hybrid regime is preferred when both full descriptions are computationally unavailable, both oracles are tractable, and its estimated cost satisfies \[C_{\mathrm{CC}}(\varepsilon)\leq\min_{m\in\mathcal M}C_m(\varepsilon),\] where \(\mathcal M\) contains eligible nonhybrid alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut–column hybrid is preferred when variables and constraints are both prohibitively numerous, pricing and separation remain tractable, and the hybrid has least estimated cost.
assumptions_latex: The finite restricted masters are solvable and provide valid bounds.
The pricing oracle detects an improving omitted generator, and the separation oracle detects a violated omitted inequality.
All costs are evaluated at the same accuracy \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The simultaneous need for pricing and separation, together with \(C_{\mathrm{CC}}(\varepsilon)\leq\min_{m\in\mathcal M}C_m(\varepsilon)\), defines the cut–column-preferred regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut–Consensus Hybrid Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural and cost conditions for combining constraint generation with scenario consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be finite and consider scenario copies \(x_s=z\) with objective \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s f_s(x_s)\). Suppose each scenario feasible set has an implicit description \(X_s=\{x:g_{si}(x)\leq0\text{ for every }i\in I_s\}\) and admits a separation oracle. A cut–consensus method alternates consensus updates with scenario-wise generation of violated valid inequalities. It is preferred when scenario subproblems parallelize, explicit enumeration of some \(I_s\) is impractical, separation is tractable, and \[C_{\mathrm{CS}}(\varepsilon)\leq\min_{m\in\mathcal M}C_m(\varepsilon).\] Generated cuts must remain valid for their scenario sets.

assumptions_latex: Each generated inequality is valid for its scenario feasible set \(X_s\).
Consensus iterations and scenario separation use compatible feasibility and accuracy tolerances.
All compared costs use the same target accuracy \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scenario separability, implicit constraints, tractable separation, and \(C_{\mathrm{CS}}(\varepsilon)\leq\min_{m\in\mathcal M}C_m(\varepsilon)\) define the cut–consensus-preferred regime.

children.title: Hybridization Selection Boundaries

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M(P)\) is finite and nonempty and contains only structurally applicable methods.
All \(C_m(P,\varepsilon)\) use one resource-accounting convention and the same fixed accuracy \(\varepsilon\).
No continuity or topology on the instance collection is assumed; consequently, a cost-tie locus is not automatically a topological boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a collection of problem instances. For each \(P\in\mathcal P\), let \(\mathcal M(P)\) be the finite nonempty set of structurally eligible methods, and let \(C_m(P,\varepsilon)\in[0,+\infty]\) be the estimated total resource cost of \(m\in\mathcal M(P)\) at common accuracy \(\varepsilon\). Define the weak and strict preference regions by \[R_m(\varepsilon)=\{P\in\mathcal P:m\in\mathcal M(P),\ C_m(P,\varepsilon)=\min_{j\in\mathcal M(P)}C_j(P,\varepsilon)\}\] and \[R_m^{\mathrm{str}}(\varepsilon)=\{P\in\mathcal P:m\in\mathcal M(P),\ C_m(P,\varepsilon)<C_j(P,\varepsilon)\text{ for every }j\in\mathcal M(P)\setminus\{m\}\}.\] For distinct methods \(m\) and \(n\), the pairwise minimum-cost tie locus is \[B_{mn}(\varepsilon)=R_m(\varepsilon)\cap R_n(\varepsilon).\] A point of this tie locus represents a selection boundary between \(m\) and \(n\) only when arbitrarily nearby instances occur in both strict preference regions under a specified topology or neighborhood structure on \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak preference region contains instances where a method attains the smallest estimated cost, while a strict region contains instances where it is the unique minimizer. The intersection of two weak regions is their minimum-cost tie locus. Such a tie is a selection boundary only when nearby instances occur on strict-preference sides for both methods.
